entries.3764aefd478e7803ecc10e3b0d3b9e3d6f33fcb3: <div sID="gen23509" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="24" osisID="Matt.24" sID="Matt.24"/> <div eID="gen23509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23510" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23511" type="x-p"/> Christ's preaching was mostly practical; but, in this chapter, we have a prophetical discourse, a prediction of things to come; such however as had a practical tendency, and was intended, not to gratify the curiosity of his disciples, but to guide their consciences and conversations, and it is therefore concluded with a practical application. The church has always had particular prophecies, besides general promises, both for direction and for encouragement to believers; but it is observable, Christ preached this prophetical sermon in the close of his ministry, as the Apocalypse is the last book of the New Testament, and the prophetical books of the Old Testament are placed last, to intimate to us, that we must be well grounded in plain truths and duties, and those must first be well digested, before we dive into those things that are dark and difficult; many run themselves into confusion by beginning their Bible at the wrong end. Now, in this chapter, we have, I. The occasion of this discourse, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.1-Matt.24.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. The discourse itself, in which we have, 1. The prophecy of divers events, especially referring to the destruction of Jerusalem, and the utter ruin of the Jewish church and nation, which were not hastening on, and were completed about forty years after; the prefaces to that destruction, the concomitants and consequences of it; yet looking further, to Christ's coming at the end of time, and the consummation of all things, of which that was a type and figure, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.4-Matt.24.31">ver. 4-31</reference>. 2. The practical application of this prophecy for the awakening and quickening of his disciples to prepare for these great and awful things, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.32-Matt.24.51">ver. 32-51</reference>.
entries.edb1bd1e96c01e819ca58c41138cdfc98859a1ef: <div eID="gen23511" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23510" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Awful Predictions.</title> <div sID="gen23512" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And Jesus went out, and departed from the temple: and his disciples came to <hi type="italic">him</hi> for to show him the buildings of the temple. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Jesus said unto them, See ye not all these things? verily I say unto you, There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down. 3 And as he sat upon the mount of Olives, the disciples came unto him privately, saying, Tell us, when shall these things be? and what <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the sign of thy coming, and of the end of the world? <div eID="gen23512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23513" type="x-p"/> Here is, <div eID="gen23513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23514" type="x-p"/> I. Christ's quitting <hi type="italic">the temple,</hi> and his public work there. He had said, in the close of the foregoing chapter, <hi type="italic">Your house is left unto you desolate;</hi> and here he made his words good; <hi type="italic">He went out, and departed from the temple.</hi> The manner of expression is observable; he not only went out of the temple, but departed from it, took his final farewell of it; he departed from it, never to return to it any more; and then immediately follows a prediction of its ruin. Note, That house is left desolate indeed, which Christ leaves. <hi type="italic">Woe unto them when I depart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.9.12">Hos. ix. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.8">Jer. vi. 8</reference>. It was now time to groan out their <hi type="italic">Ichabod, The glory is departed, their defence is departed.</hi> Three days after this, the veil of the temple was rent; when Christ left it, all became <hi type="italic">common and unclean;</hi> but Christ departed not till they drove him away; did not reject them, till they first rejected him. <div eID="gen23514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23515" type="x-p"/> II. His private discourse with his disciples; he left the temple, but he did not leave the twelve, who were the seed of the gospel church, which the casting off of the Jews was the enriching of. When he left the temple, his disciples left it too, and came to him. Note, It is good being where Christ is, and leaving that which he leaves. They came to him, to be instructed in private, when his public preaching was over; for <hi type="italic">the secret of the Lord is with them that fear him.</hi> He had spoken of the destruction of the Jewish church to the multitude in parables, which here, as usual, he explains to his disciples. Observe, <div eID="gen23515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23516" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">His disciples came to him, to show him the buildings of the temple,</hi> It was a stately and beautiful structure, one of the wonders of the world; no cost was spared, no art left untried, to make it sumptuous. Though it came short of Solomon's temple, and <hi type="italic">its beginning was small,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">its latter end did greatly increase.</hi> It was richly furnished with gifts and offerings, to which there were continual additions made. They showed Christ these things, and desired him to take notice of them, either, <div eID="gen23516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23517" type="x-p"/> (1.) As being greatly pleased with them themselves, and expecting he should be so too. They had lived mostly in Galilee, at a distance from the temple, had seldom seen it, and therefore were the more struck with admiration at it, and thought he should admire as much as they did <hi type="italic">all this glory</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.1">Gen. xxxi. 1</reference>); and they would have him divert himself (after his preaching, and from his sorrow which they saw him perhaps almost overwhelmed with) with looking about him. Note, Even good men are apt to be too much enamoured with outward pomp and gaiety, and to overvalue it, even in the things of God; whereas we should be, as Christ was, dead to it, and look upon it with contempt. The temple was indeed glorious, but, [1.] Its glory was sullied and stained with the sin of the priests and people; that wicked doctrine of the Pharisees, which preferred the gold before the temple that sanctified it, was enough to deface the beauty of all the ornaments of the temple. [2.] Its glory was eclipsed and outdone by the presence of Christ in it, who was <hi type="italic">the glory of this latter house</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.9">Hag. ii. 9</reference>), so that the buildings had no glory, in comparison with that glory which excelled. <div eID="gen23517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23518" type="x-p"/> Or, (2.) As grieving that this house should be left desolate; they showed him the buildings, as if they would move him to reverse the sentence; "Lord, let not this holy and beautiful house, where our fathers praised thee, be made a desolation." They forgot how many providences, concerning Solomon's temple, had manifested how little God cared for that outward glory which they had so much admired, when the people were wicked, <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.21">2 Chron. vii. 21</reference>. <hi type="italic">This house, which is high,</hi> sin will bring low. Christ had lately looked upon <hi type="italic">the precious souls, and wept for them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.19.41">Luke xix. 41</reference>. The disciples look upon the pompous buildings, and are ready to weep for them. In this, as in other things, <hi type="italic">his thoughts are not like ours.</hi> It was weakness, and meanness of spirit, in the disciples, to be so fond of fine buildings; it was a childish thing. <hi type="italic">Animo magno nihil magnum—To a great mind nothing is great.</hi> Seneca. <div eID="gen23518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23519" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ, hereupon, foretels the utter ruin and destruction that were coming upon this place, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.2">v. 2</reference>. Note, A believing foresight of the defacing of all worldly glory will help to take us off from admiring it, and overvaluing it. The most beautiful body will be shortly worms' meat, and the most beautiful building a ruinous heap. And shall we then set our eyes upon that which so soon is not, and look upon that with so much admiration which ere long we shall certainly look upon with so much contempt? <hi type="italic">See ye not all these things?</hi> They would have Christ look upon them, and be as much in love with them as they were; he would have them look upon them, and be as dead to them as he was. There is such a sight of these things as will do us good; so to see them as to see through them and see to the end of them. <div eID="gen23519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23520" type="x-p"/> Christ, instead of reversing the decree, ratifies it; <hi type="italic">Verily, I say unto you, there shall not be left one stone upon another.</hi> <div eID="gen23520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23521" type="x-p"/> (1.) He speaks of it as a certain ruin; "<hi type="italic">I say unto you. I,</hi> that know what I say, and know how to make good what I say; take my word for it, it shall be so; <hi type="italic">I, the Amen, the true Witness, say it to you.</hi>" All judgment being committed to the Son, the threatenings, as well as the promises, are all <hi type="italic">yea, and amen, in him.</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.6.17-Heb.6.18">Heb. vi. 17, 18</reference>. <div eID="gen23521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23522" type="x-p"/> (2.) He speaks of it as an utter ruin. The temple shall not only be stripped, and plundered, and defaced, but utterly demolished and laid waste; <hi type="italic">Not one stone shall be left upon another.</hi> Notice is taken, in the <hi type="italic">building</hi> of the second temple, of the <hi type="italic">laying of one stone upon another</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.15">Hag. ii. 15</reference>); and here, in the <hi type="italic">ruin,</hi> of <hi type="italic">not leaving one stone upon another.</hi> History tells us, that this was fulfilled in the latter; for though Titus, when he took the city, did all he could to preserve the temple, yet he could not restrain the enraged soldiers from destroying it utterly; and it was done to that degree, that Turnus Rufus ploughed up the ground on which it had stood: thus that scripture was fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Mic.3.12">Mic. iii. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">Zion shall, for your sake, be ploughed as a field.</hi> And afterward, in Julian the Apostate's time, when the Jews were encouraged by him to rebuild their temple, in opposition to the Christian religion, what remained of the ruins was quite pulled down, to level the ground for a new foundation; but the attempt was defeated by the miraculous eruption of fire out of the ground, which destroyed the foundation they laid, and frightened away the builders. Now this prediction of the final and irreparable ruin of the temple includes a prediction of the period of the Levitical priesthood and the ceremonial law. <div eID="gen23522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23523" type="x-p"/> 3. The disciples, not disputing either the truth or the equity of this sentence, nor doubting of the accomplishment of it, enquire more particularly of the time when it should come to pass, and the signs of its approach, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.3">v. 3</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen23523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23524" type="x-p"/> (1.) Where they made this enquiry; privately, <hi type="italic">as he sat upon the mount of Olives;</hi> probably, he was returning to Bethany, and there sat down by the way, to rest him; the mount of Olives directly faced the temple, and from thence he might have a full prospect of it at some distance; there he sat as a Judge upon the bench, the temple and city being before him as at the bar, and thus he passed sentence on them. We read (<reference osisRef="Ezek.11.23">Ezek. xi. 23</reference>) of the removing of the glory of the Lord from the temple to the mountain; so Christ, the great Shechinah, here removes to this mountain. <div eID="gen23524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23525" type="x-p"/> (2.) What the enquiry itself was; <hi type="italic">When shall these things be; and what shall be the sign of thy coming, and of the end of the world?</hi> Here are three questions. <div eID="gen23525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23526" type="x-p"/> [1.] Some think, these questions do all point at one and the same thing—the destruction of the temple, and the period of the Jewish church and nation, which Christ had himself spoken of as his coming (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.28">ch. xvi. 28</reference>), and which would be the consummation of the age (for so it may be read), the finishing of that dispensation. Or, they thought the destruction of the temple must needs be the end of the world. If that house be laid waste, the world cannot stand; for the Rabbin used to say that the house of the sanctuary was one of the seven things for the sake of which the world was made; and they think, if so, the world will not survive the temple. <div eID="gen23526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23527" type="x-p"/> [2.] Others think their question, <hi type="italic">When shall these things be?</hi> refers to the destruction of Jerusalem, and the other two to the end of the world; or Christ's coming may refer to his setting up his gospel kingdom, and the end of the world to the day of judgment. I rather incline to think that their question looked no further than the event Christ now foretold; but it appears by other passages, that they had very confused thoughts of future events; so that perhaps it is not possible to put any certain construction upon this question of theirs. <div eID="gen23527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23528" type="x-p"/> But Christ, in his answer, though he does not expressly rectify the mistakes of his disciples (that must be done by the pouring out of the Spirit), yet looks further than their question, and instructs his church, not only concerning the great events of that age, the destruction of Jerusalem, but concerning his second coming at the end of time, which here he insensibly slides into a discourse of, and of that it is plain he speaks in the next chapter, which is a continuation of this sermon.
entries.bc0eab1709b0afbf06c0da46960ea2001a241619: <div eID="gen23528" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Awful Predictions.</title> <div sID="gen23529" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> And Jesus answered and said unto them, Take heed that no man deceive you. <hi type="super">5</hi> For many shall come in my name, saying, I am Christ; and shall deceive many. <hi type="super">6</hi> And ye shall hear of wars and rumours of wars: see that ye be not troubled: for all <hi type="italic">these things</hi> must come to pass, but the end is not yet. <hi type="super">7</hi> For nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom: and there shall be famines, and pestilences, and earthquakes, in divers places. <hi type="super">8</hi> All these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the beginning of sorrows. <hi type="super">9</hi> Then shall they deliver you up to be afflicted, and shall kill you: and ye shall be hated of all nations for my name's sake. <hi type="super">10</hi> And then shall many be offended, and shall betray one another, and shall hate one another. <hi type="super">11</hi> And many false prophets shall rise, and shall deceive many. <hi type="super">12</hi> And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold. <hi type="super">13</hi> But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved. <hi type="super">14</hi> And this gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in all the world for a witness unto all nations; and then shall the end come. <hi type="super">15</hi> When ye therefore shall see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, stand in the holy place, (whoso readeth, let him understand:) <hi type="super">16</hi> Then let them which be in Judea flee into the mountains: <hi type="super">17</hi> Let him which is on the housetop not come down to take any thing out of his house: <hi type="super">18</hi> Neither let him which is in the field return back to take his clothes. <hi type="super">19</hi> And woe unto them that are with child, and to them that give suck in those days! <hi type="super">20</hi> But pray ye that your flight be not in the winter, neither on the sabbath day: <hi type="super">21</hi> For then shall be great tribulation, such as was not since the beginning of the world to this time, no, nor ever shall be. <hi type="super">22</hi> And except those days should be shortened, there should no flesh be saved: but for the elect's sake those days shall be shortened. <hi type="super">23</hi> Then if any man shall say unto you, Lo, here <hi type="italic">is</hi> Christ, or there; believe <hi type="italic">it</hi> not. <hi type="super">24</hi> For there shall arise false Christs, and false prophets, and shall show great signs and wonders; insomuch that, if <hi type="italic">it were</hi> possible, they shall deceive the very elect. <hi type="super">25</hi> Behold, I have told you before. 26 Wherefore if they shall say unto you, Behold, he is in the desert; go not forth: behold, <hi type="italic">he is</hi> in the secret chambers; believe <hi type="italic">it</hi> not. <hi type="super">27</hi> For as the lightning cometh out of the east, and shineth even unto the west; so shall also the coming of the Son of man be. <hi type="super">28</hi> For wheresoever the carcase is, there will the eagles be gathered together. <hi type="super">29</hi> Immediately after the tribulation of those days shall the sun be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens shall be shaken: <hi type="super">30</hi> And then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven: and then shall all the tribes of the earth mourn, and they shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. <hi type="super">31</hi> And he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other. <div eID="gen23529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23530" type="x-p"/> The disciples had asked concerning the times, <hi type="italic">When shall these things be?</hi> Christ gives them no answer to that, after what number of days and years his prediction should be accomplished, for <hi type="italic">it is not for us to know the times</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.7">Acts i. 7</reference>); but they had asked, <hi type="italic">What shall be the sign?</hi> That question he answers fully, for we are concerned to <hi type="italic">understand the signs of the times,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.16.3">ch. xvi. 3</reference>. Now the prophecy primarily respects the events near at hand—the destruction of Jerusalem, the period of the Jewish church and state, the calling of the Gentiles, and the setting up of Christ's kingdom in the world; but as the prophecies of the Old Testament, which have an immediate reference to the affairs of the Jews and the revolutions of their state, under the figure of them do certainly look further, to the gospel church and the kingdom of the Messiah, and are so expounded in the New Testament, and such expressions are found in those predictions as are peculiar thereto and not applicable otherwise; so this prophecy, under the type of Jerusalem's destruction, looks as far forward as the general judgment; and, as is usual in prophecies, some passages are most applicable to the type, and others to the antitype; and toward the close, as usual, it points more particularly to the latter. It is observable, that what Christ here saith to his disciples tends more to engage their caution than to satisfy their curiosity; more to prepare them for the events that should happen than to give them a distinct idea of the events themselves. This is that good understanding of the time which we should all covet, thence to infer what Israel ought to do: and so this prophecy is of standing lasting use to the church, and will be so to the end of time; for <hi type="italic">the thing that hath been, is that which shall be</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.5-Eccl.1.7">Eccl. i. 5, 6, 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.9">9</reference>), and the series, connection, and presages, of events, are much the same still that they were then; so that upon the prophecy of this chapter, pointing at that event, moral prognostications may be made, and such constructions of the signs of the times as the wise man's heart will know how to improve. <div eID="gen23530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23531" type="x-p"/> I. Christ here foretels the going forth of deceivers; he begins with a caution, <hi type="italic">Take heed that no man deceive you.</hi> They expected to be told when these things should be, to be let into that secret; but this caution is a check to their curiosity, "<hi type="italic">What is that to you?</hi> Mind you your duty, follow me, and be not seduced from following me." Those that are most inquisitive concerning the secret things which belong not to them are most easily imposed upon by seducers, <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.3">2 Thess. ii. 3</reference>. The disciples, when they heard that the Jews, their most inveterate enemies, should be destroyed, might be in danger of falling into security; "Nay," saith Christ, "you are more exposed other ways." Seducers are more dangerous enemies to the church than persecutors. <div eID="gen23531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23532" type="x-p"/> Three times in this discourse he mentions the appearing of <hi type="italic">false prophets,</hi> which was, 1. A presage of Jerusalem's ruin. Justly were they who killed the true prophets, left to be ensnared by false prophets; and they who crucified the true Messiah, left to be deceived and broken by false Christs and pretended Messiahs. The appearing of these was the occasion of dividing that people into parties and factions, which made their ruin the more easy and speedy; and the sin of the many that were led aside by them, helped to fill the measure. 2. It was a trial to the disciples of Christ, and therefore agreeable to their state of probation, <hi type="italic">that they which are perfect, may be made manifest.</hi> <div eID="gen23532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23533" type="x-p"/> Now concerning these deceivers, observe here, <div eID="gen23533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23534" type="x-p"/> (1.) The pretences they should come under. Satan acts most mischievously, when he appears as an angel of light: the colour of the greatest good is often the cover of the greatest evil. <div eID="gen23534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23535" type="x-p"/> [1.] There should appear <hi type="italic">false prophets</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.11-Matt.24.24">v. 11-24</reference>); the deceivers would pretend to divine inspiration, an immediate mission, and a spirit of prophecy, when it was all a lie. Such they had been formerly (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.16">Jer. xxiii. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.6">Ezek. xiii. 6</reference>), as was foretold, <reference osisRef="Deut.13.3">Deut. xiii. 3</reference>. Some think, the seducers here pointed to were such as had been settled teachers in the church, and had gained reputation as such, but afterward betrayed the truth they had taught, and revolted to error; and from such the danger is the greater, because least suspected. One false traitor in the garrison may do more mischief than a thousand avowed enemies without. <div eID="gen23535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23536" type="x-p"/> [2.] There should appear <hi type="italic">false Christs, coming in Christ's name</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.5">v. 5</reference>), assuming to themselves the name peculiar to him, and saying, <hi type="italic">I am Christ, pseudo-christs,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.24">v. 24</reference>. There was at that time a general expectation of the appearing of the Messiah; they spoke of him; as <hi type="italic">he that should come;</hi> but when he did come, the body of the nation rejected him; which those who were ambitious of making themselves a name, took advantage of, and set up for Christ. Josephus speaks of several such impostors between this and the destruction of Jerusalem; one Theudas, that was defeated by Cospius Fadus; another by Felix, another by Festus. Dosetheus said he was the Christ foretold by Moses. <hi type="italic">Origen adversus Celsum.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Acts.5.36-Acts.5.37">Acts v. 36, 37</reference>. Simon Magus pretended to be <hi type="italic">the great power of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.8.10">Acts viii. 10</reference>. In after-ages there have been such pretenders; one about a hundred years after Christ, that called himself <hi type="italic">Bar-cochobas—The son of a star,</hi> but proved <hi type="italic">Bar-cosba—The son of a lie.</hi> About fifty years ago Sabbati-Levi set up for a Messiah in the Turkish empire, and was greatly caressed by the Jews; but in a short time <hi type="italic">his folly was made manifest.</hi> See Sir Paul Rycaut's <hi type="italic">History.</hi> The popish religion doth, in effect, set up a false Christ; the Pope comes, in Christ's name, as his vicar, but invades and usurps all his offices, and so is a rival with him, and, as such, an enemy to him, a deceiver, and an antichrist. <div eID="gen23536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23537" type="x-p"/> [3.] These false Christs and false prophets would have their agents and emissaries busy in all places to draw people in to them, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.23">v. 23</reference>. <hi type="italic">Then</hi> when public troubles are great and threatening, and people will be catching at any thing that looks like deliverance, then Satan will take the advantage of imposing on them; they will say, <hi type="italic">Lo, here is a Christ, or there</hi> is one; but do not mind them: the true Christ did not strive, nor cry; nor was it said of him, <hi type="italic">Lo, here! or Lo, there!</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.17.21">Luke xvii. 21</reference>), therefore if any man say so concerning him, look upon it as a temptation. The hermits, who place religion in a monastical life, say, <hi type="italic">He is in the desert;</hi> the priests, who made the consecrated wafer to be Christ, say, "He is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">en tois tameiois</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">in the cupboards, in the secret chambers:</hi> lo, he is in this shrine, in that image." Thus some appropriate Christ's spiritual presence to one party or persuasion, as if they had the monopoly of Christ and Christianity; and the kingdom of Christ must stand and fall, must live and die, with them; "Lo, he is in this church, in that council:" whereas Christ is All in all, not here or there, but meets his people with a blessing <hi type="italic">in every place where he records his name.</hi> <div eID="gen23537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23538" type="x-p"/> (2.) The proof they should offer for the making good of these pretences; <hi type="italic">They shall show great signs and wonders</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.24">v. 24</reference>), not true miracles, those are a divine seal, and with those the doctrine of Christ stands confirmed; and therefore if any offer to draw us from that by signs and wonders, we must have recourse to that rule given of old (<reference osisRef="Deut.13.1-Deut.13.3">Deut. xiii. 1-3</reference>), <hi type="italic">If the sign or wonder come to pass,</hi> yet follow not him that would draw you <hi type="italic">to serve other gods,</hi> or believe in other Christs, <hi type="italic">for the Lord your God proveth you.</hi> But these were <hi type="italic">lying wonders</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.9">2 Thess. ii. 9</reference>), wrought by Satan (God permitting him), who is <hi type="italic">the prince of the power of the air.</hi> It is not said, <hi type="italic">They shall work miracles,</hi> but, <hi type="italic">They shall show great signs;</hi> they are but a show; either they impose upon men's credulity by false narratives, or deceive their senses by tricks of legerdemain, or arts of divination, as the magicians of Egypt by their enchantments. <div eID="gen23538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23539" type="x-p"/> (3.) The success they should have in these attempts, <div eID="gen23539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23540" type="x-p"/> [1.] <hi type="italic">They shall deceive many</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.5">v. 5</reference>), and again, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.11">v. 11</reference>. Note, The devil and his instruments may prevail far in deceiving poor souls; few find the strait gate, but many are drawn into the broad way; many will be imposed upon by their signs and wonders, and many drawn in by the hopes of deliverance from their oppressions. Note, Neither miracles nor multitudes are certain signs of a true church; for <hi type="italic">all the world wonders after the beast,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.13.3">Rev. xiii. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen23540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23541" type="x-p"/> [2.] <hi type="italic">They shall deceive, if it were possible, the very elect,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.24">v. 24</reference>. This bespeaks, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The strength of the delusion; it is such as many shall be carried away by (so strong shall the stream be), even those that were thought to stand fast. Men's knowledge, gifts, learning, eminent station, and long profession, will not secure them; but, notwithstanding these, many will be deceived; nothing but the almighty grace of God, pursuant to his eternal purpose, will be a protection. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The safety of the elect in the midst of this danger, which is taken for granted in that parenthesis, <hi type="italic">If it were possible,</hi> plainly implying that it is not possible, for they are <hi type="italic">kept by the power of God,</hi> that <hi type="italic">the purpose of God, according to the election, may stand.</hi> It is possible for those that have been enlightened to fall away (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.4-Heb.6.6">Heb. vi. 4, 5, 6</reference>), but not for those that were elected. If God's chosen ones should be deceived, God's choice would be defeated, which is not to be imagined, <hi type="italic">for whom he did predestinate, he called, justified, and glorified,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.30">Rom. viii. 30</reference>. They were given to Christ; and of all that were given to him, he will lose none, <reference osisRef="John.10.28">John x. 28</reference>. Grotius will have this to be meant of the great difficulty of drawing the primitive Christians from their religion, and quotes it as used proverbially by Galen; when he would express a thing very difficult and morally impossible, he saith, "You may sooner draw away a Christian from Christ." <div eID="gen23541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23542" type="x-p"/> (4.) The repeated cautions which our Saviour gives to his disciples to stand upon their guard against them; <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he gave them warning, that they might watch ( <reference osisRef="Matt.24.25">v. 25</reference>); <hi type="italic">Behold, I have told you before.</hi> He that is told before where he will be assaulted, may save himself, as the king of Israel did, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.9-2Kgs.6.10">2 Kings vi. 9, 10</reference>. Note, Christ's warnings are designed to engage our watchfulness; and though the elect shall be preserved from delusion, yet they shall be preserved by the use of appointed means, and a due regard to the cautions of the word; we are kept through faith, faith in Christ's word, which he has told us before. <div eID="gen23542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23543" type="x-p"/> [1.] We must not believe those who say, <hi type="italic">Lo, here is Christ;</hi> or, <hi type="italic">Lo, he is there,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.23">v. 23</reference>. We believe that the true Christ is at the right hand of God, and that his spiritual presence is <hi type="italic">where two or three are gathered together in his name;</hi> believe not those therefore who would draw you off from a Christ in heaven, by telling you he is any where on earth; or draw you off from the catholic church on earth, by telling you he is here, or he is there; believe it not. Note, There is not a greater enemy to true faith than vain credulity. The simple believeth every word, and runs after every cry. <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Memneso apistein</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Beware of believing.</hi> <div eID="gen23543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23544" type="x-p"/> [2.] We must not go forth after those that say, <hi type="italic">He is in the desert,</hi> or, <hi type="italic">He is in the secret chambers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.26">v. 26</reference>. We must not hearken to every empiric and pretender, nor follow every one that puts up the finger to point us to a new Christ, and a new gospel; "Go not forth, for if you do, you are in danger of being taken by them; therefore keep out of harm's way, <hi type="italic">be not carried about with every wind;</hi> many a man's vain curiosity to go forth hath led him into a fatal apostasy; your strength at such a time is to sit still, to have the heart established with grace." <div eID="gen23544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23545" type="x-p"/> II. He foretels wars and great commotions among the nations, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.6-Matt.24.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. When Christ was born, there was a universal peace in the empire, the temple of Janus was shut; but <hi type="italic">think not that Christ came to send,</hi> or continue such a <hi type="italic">peace</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.51">Luke xii. 51</reference>); no, his city and his wall are to be built even in troublesome times, and even wars shall forward his work. From the time that the Jews rejected Christ, and he <hi type="italic">left their house desolate, the sword did never depart from their house, the sword of the Lord</hi> was never quiet, because he had given it a charge against a hypocritical nation and the people of his wrath, and by it brought ruin upon them. <div eID="gen23545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23546" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A prediction of the event of the day; You will now shortly <hi type="italic">hear of wars, and rumours of wars.</hi> When wars are, they will be heard; for <hi type="italic">every battle of the warrior is with confused noise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.9.5">Isa. ix. 5</reference>. See how terrible it is (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.19">Jer. iv. 19</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou hast heard, O my soul, the alarm of war!</hi> Even the quiet in the land, and the least inquisitive after new things, cannot but hear the rumours of war. See what comes of refusing the gospel! Those that will not hear the messengers of peace, shall be made to hear the messengers of war. God has a sword ready to avenge the quarrel of his covenant, his new covenant. <hi type="italic">Nation shall rise up against nation,</hi> that is, one part or province of the Jewish nation against another, one city against another (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.5-2Chr.15.6">2 Chron. xv. 5, 6</reference>); and in the same province and city one party or faction shall rise up against another, so that they shall be devoured by, and dashed in pieces against one another, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.19-Isa.9.21">Isa. ix. 19-21</reference>. <div eID="gen23546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23547" type="x-p"/> 2. A prescription of the duty of the day; <hi type="italic">See that ye be not troubled.</hi> Is it possible to hear such sad news, and not be troubled? Yet, where the heart is fixed, trusting in God, it is kept in peace, and is not afraid, no not of the evil tidings of wars, and rumours of wars; no not the noise of <hi type="italic">Arm, arm. Be not troubled;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Me throeithe</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Be not put into confusion or commotion;</hi> not put into throes, as a woman with child by a fright; <hi type="italic">see that ye be not</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">orate</hi></hi>. Note, There is need of constant care and watchfulness to keep trouble from the heart when there are wars abroad; and it is against the mind of Christ, that his people should have troubled hearts even in troublous times. <div eID="gen23547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23548" type="x-p"/> We must not be troubled, for two reasons. <div eID="gen23548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23549" type="x-p"/> (1.) Because we are bid to expect this: the Jews must be punished, ruin must be brought upon them; by this the justice of God and the honour of the Redeemer must be asserted; and therefore <hi type="italic">all those things must come to pass;</hi> the word is gone out of God's mouth, and it shall be accomplished in its season. Note, The consideration of the unchangeableness of the divine counsels, which govern all events, should compose and quiet our spirits, whatever happens. God is but performing the thing that is appointed for us, and our inordinate trouble is an interpretative quarrel with that appointment. Let us therefore acquiesce, because <hi type="italic">these things must come to pass;</hi> not only <hi type="italic">necessitate decreti—as the product of the divine counsel,</hi> but <hi type="italic">necessitate medii—as a means in order to a further end.</hi> The old house must be taken down (though it cannot be done without noise, and dust, and danger), ere the new fabric can be erected: the things that are shaken (and ill shaken they were) <hi type="italic">must be removed, that the things which cannot be shaken may remain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.27">Heb. xii. 27</reference>. <div eID="gen23549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23550" type="x-p"/> (2.) Because we are still to expect worse; <hi type="italic">The end is not yet;</hi> the end of time is not, and, while time lasts, we must expect trouble, and that the end of one affliction will be but the beginning of another; or, "The end of these troubles is not yet; there must be more judgments that one made use of to bring down the Jewish power; more vials of wrath must yet be poured out; there is but one woe past, more woes are yet to come, more arrows are yet to be spent upon them out of God's quiver; therefore be not troubled, do not give way to fear and trouble, sink not under the present burthen, but rather gather in all the strength and spirit you have, to encounter what is yet before you. Be not troubled to hear of wars and rumours of wars; for then what will become of you when the famines and pestilences come?" If it be to us a vexation but to <hi type="italic">understand the report</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.19">Isa. xxviii. 19</reference>), what will it be to feel the stroke when it <hi type="italic">toucheth the bone and the flesh?</hi> If running with the footmen weary us, how shall we contend with horses? And if we be frightened at a little brook in our way, <hi type="italic">what shall we do in the swellings of Jordan?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.12.5">Jer. xii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen23550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23551" type="x-p"/> III. He foretels other judgments more immediately sent of God—<hi type="italic">famines, pestilences, and earthquakes.</hi> Famine is often the effect of war, and pestilence of famine. These were the three judgments which David was to choose one out of; and he was in a great strait, for he knew not which was the worst: but what dreadful desolations will they make, when they all pour in together upon a people! Beside war (and that is enough), there shall be, <div eID="gen23551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23552" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">Famine,</hi> signified by the <hi type="italic">black horse</hi> under the <hi type="italic">third seal,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.6.5-Rev.6.6">Rev. vi. 5, 6</reference>. We read of a famine in Judea, not long after Christ's time, which was very impoverishing (<reference osisRef="Acts.11.28">Acts xi. 28</reference>); but the sorest famine was in Jerusalem during the siege. See <reference osisRef="Lam.4.9-Lam.4.10">Lam. iv. 9, 10</reference>. <div eID="gen23552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23553" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">Pestilences,</hi> signified by the <hi type="italic">pale horse, and death upon him,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the grave at his heels,</hi> under the <hi type="italic">fourth seal,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.6.7-Rev.6.8">Rev. vi. 7, 8</reference>. This destroys without distinction, and in a little time lays heaps upon heaps. <div eID="gen23553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23554" type="x-p"/> 3. <hi type="italic">Earthquakes in divers places,</hi> or from place to place, pursuing those that flee from them, as they did from the earthquake <hi type="italic">in the days of Uzziah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.14.5">Zech. xiv. 5</reference>. Great desolations have sometimes been made by earthquakes, of late and formerly; they have been the death of many, and the terror of more. In the apocalyptic visions, it is observable, that earthquakes bode good, and no evil, to the church, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.12">Rev. vi. 12</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="Rev.6.15 Rev.11.12-Rev.11.13 Rev.11.19 Rev.16.17-Rev.16.19">Rev. vi. 15; xi. 12, 13, 19; xvi. 17-19</reference>. When God <hi type="italic">shakes terribly the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.21">Isa. ii. 21</reference>), it is to <hi type="italic">shake the wicked out of it</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.38.13">Job xxxviii. 13</reference>), and to introduce <hi type="italic">the desire of all nations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hag.2.6-Hag.2.7">Hag. ii. 6, 7</reference>. But here they are spoken of as dreadful judgments, and yet but <hi type="italic">the beginning of sorrows,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">odinon</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">of travailing pains,</hi> quick, violent, yet tedious too. Note, When God judgeth, he will overcome; <hi type="italic">when he begins</hi> in wrath, <hi type="italic">he will make</hi> a full <hi type="italic">end,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.12">1 Sam. iii. 12</reference>. When we look forward to the eternity of misery that is before the obstinate refusers of Christ and his gospel, we may truly say, concerning the greatest temporal judgments, "They are but the beginning of sorrows; bad as things are with them, there are worse behind." <div eID="gen23554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23555" type="x-p"/> IV. He foretels the persecution of his own people and ministers, and a general apostasy and decay in religion thereupon, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.9-Matt.24.10">v. 9, 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.12">12</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen23555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23556" type="x-p"/> 1. The <hi type="italic">cross</hi> itself foretold, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.9">v. 9</reference>. Note, Of all future events we are as much concerned, though commonly as little desirous, to know of our own sufferings as of any thing else. <hi type="italic">Then,</hi> when famines and pestilences prevail, then they shall impute them to the Christians, and make that a pretence for persecuting them; <hi type="italic">Christianos ad leones—Away with Christians to the lions.</hi> Christ had told his disciples, when he first sent them out, what hard things they should suffer; but they had hitherto experienced little of it, and therefore he reminds them again, that the less they had suffered, the more there was behind to be filled up, <reference osisRef="Col.1.24">Col. i. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen23556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23557" type="x-p"/> (1.) They shall be <hi type="italic">afflicted</hi> with bonds and imprisonments, <hi type="italic">cruel mockings and scourgings,</hi> as blessed Paul (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.23-2Cor.11.25">2 Cor. xi. 23-25</reference>); not killed outright, but <hi type="italic">killed all the day long, in deaths often,</hi> killed so as to feel themselves die, <hi type="italic">made a spectacle to the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.9">1 Cor. iv. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.11">11</reference>. <div eID="gen23557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23558" type="x-p"/> (2.) They shall be <hi type="italic">killed;</hi> so cruel are the church's enemies, that nothing less will satisfy them than the blood of the saints, which they thirst after, suck, and shed, like water. <div eID="gen23558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23559" type="x-p"/> (3.) They shall be <hi type="italic">hated of all nations for Christ's name's sake,</hi> as he had told them before, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.22">ch. x. 22</reference>. The world was generally leavened with enmity and malignity to Christians: the Jews, though spiteful to the Heathen, were never persecuted by them as the Christians were; they were hated by the Jews that were dispersed among the nations, were the common butt of the world's malice. What shall we think of this world, when the best men had the worst usage in it? It is the cause that makes the martyr, and comforts him; it was for Christ's sake that they were thus hated; their professing and preaching his name incensed the nations so much against them; the devil, finding a fatal shock thereby given to his kingdom, and that his time was likely to be short, <hi type="italic">came down, having great wrath.</hi> <div eID="gen23559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23560" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">The offence of the cross,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.10-Matt.24.12">v. 10-12</reference>. Satan thus carries on his interest by force of arms, though Christ, at length, will bring glory to himself out of the sufferings of his people and ministers. Three ill effects of persecution are here foretold. <div eID="gen23560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23561" type="x-p"/> (1.) The <hi type="italic">apostasy</hi> of some. When the profession of Christianity begins to cost men dear, <hi type="italic">then shall many be offended,</hi> shall first fall out with, and then fall off from, their profession; they will begin to pick quarrels with their religion, sit loose to it, grow weary of it, and at length revolt from it. Note, [1.] It is no new thing (though it is a strange thing) for those that have known the way of righteousness, to turn aside out of it. Paul often complains of deserters, who began well, but something hindered them. They were with us, but went out from us, because never truly of us, <reference osisRef="1John.2.19">1 John ii. 19</reference>. We are told of it before. [2.] Suffering times are shaking times; and those fall in the storm, that stood in fair weather, like the <hi type="italic">stony ground hearers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.13.21">ch. xiii. 21</reference>. Many will follow Christ in the sunshine, who will shift for themselves, and leave him to do so to, in the cloudy dark day. They like their religion while they can have it cheap, and sleep with it in a whole skin; but, if their profession cost them any thing, they quit it presently. <div eID="gen23561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23562" type="x-p"/> (2.) The <hi type="italic">malignity</hi> of others. When persecution is in fashion, envy, enmity, and malice, are strangely diffused into the minds of men by contagion: and charity, tenderness, and moderation, are looked upon as singularities, which make a man like a speckled bird. Then <hi type="italic">they shall betray one another,</hi> that is,"Those that have treacherously deserted their religion, shall hate and betray those who adhere to it, for whom they have pretended friendship." Apostates have commonly been the most bitter and violent persecutors. Note, Persecuting times are discovering times. Wolves in sheep's clothing will then throw off their disguise, and appear wolves: they shall <hi type="italic">betray one another, and hate one another.</hi> The times must needs be perilous, when treachery and hatred, two of the worst things that can be, because directly contrary to two of the best (truth and love), shall have the ascendant. This seems to refer to the barbarous treatment which the several contending factions among the Jews gave to one another; and justly were they who ate up God's people as they ate bread, left thus to bite and devour one another till they were <hi type="italic">consumed one of another;</hi> or, it may refer to the mischiefs done to Christ's disciples by those that were nearest to them, as <reference osisRef="Matt.10.21">ch. x. 21</reference>. <hi type="italic">The brother shall deliver up the brother to death.</hi> <div eID="gen23562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23563" type="x-p"/> (3.) The general <hi type="italic">declining</hi> and <hi type="italic">cooling</hi> of most, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.12">v. 12</reference>. In seducing times, when false prophets arise, in persecuting times, when the saints are hated, expect these two things, <div eID="gen23563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23564" type="x-p"/> [1.] The <hi type="italic">abounding</hi> of iniquity; though the world always lies in wickedness, yet there are some times in which it may be said, that <hi type="italic">iniquity doth</hi> in a special manner abound; as when it is more extensive than ordinary, as in the old world, when <hi type="italic">all flesh had corrupted their way;</hi> and when it is more <hi type="italic">excessive</hi> than ordinary, when <hi type="italic">violence is risen up to a rod of wickedness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.11">Ezek. vii. 11</reference>), so that hell seems to be broke loose in blasphemies against God, and enmities to the saints. <div eID="gen23564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23565" type="x-p"/> [2.] The <hi type="italic">abating</hi> of love; this is the consequence of the former; <hi type="italic">Because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold.</hi> Understand it in general of true serious godliness, which is all summed up in <hi type="italic">love;</hi> it is too common for professors of religion to grow cool in their profession, when the wicked are hot in their wickedness; as the church of Ephesus in bad times <hi type="italic">left her first love,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.2.2-Rev.2.4">Rev. ii. 2-4</reference>. Or, it may be understood more particularly of brotherly love. When iniquity abounds, seducing iniquity, persecuting iniquity, this grace commonly waxes cold. Christians begin to be shy and suspicious one of another, affections are alienated, distances created, parties made, and so love comes to nothing. The devil is the accuser of the brethren, not only to their enemies, which makes persecuting iniquity abound, but one to another, which makes the love of many to wax cold. <div eID="gen23565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23566" type="x-p"/> This gives a melancholy prospect of the times, that there shall be such a great decay of love; but, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is of the love of <hi type="italic">many,</hi> not of <hi type="italic">all.</hi> In the worst of times, God has his remnant that hold fast their integrity, and retain their zeal, as in Elijah's days, when he thought himself left alone. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> This love is grown cold, but not dead; it abates, but is not quite cast off. There is life in the root, which will show itself when the winter is past. The new nature may <hi type="italic">wax cold,</hi> but shall not <hi type="italic">wax old,</hi> for then it would decay and vanish away. <div eID="gen23566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23567" type="x-p"/> 3. Comfort administered in reference to this offence of the cross, for the support of the Lord's people under it (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.13">v. 13</reference>); <hi type="italic">He that endures to the end, shall be saved.</hi> (1.) It is comfortable to those who wish well to the cause of Christ in general, that, though many are offended, yet some shall endure to the end. When we see so many drawing back, we are ready to fear that the cause of Christ will sink for want of supporters, and his name be left and forgotten for want of some to make profession of it; but even at this time there is <hi type="italic">a remnant according to the election of grace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.5">Rom. xi. 5</reference>. It is spoken of the same time that this prophecy has reference to; a remnant who are not of <hi type="italic">them that draw back unto perdition,</hi> but believe and persevere <hi type="italic">to the saving of the soul;</hi> they endure to the end, to the end of their lives, to the end of their present state of probation, or to the end of these suffering trying times, to the last encounter, though they should be called to resist unto blood. (2.) It is comfortable to those who do thus endure to the end, and suffer for their constancy, that they shall be saved. Perseverance wins the crown, through free grace, and shall wear it. <hi type="italic">They shall be saved:</hi> perhaps they may be delivered out of their troubles, and comfortably survive them in this world; but it is eternal salvation that is here intended. They that endure to the end of their days, shall then receive the end of their faith and hope, <hi type="italic">even the salvation of their souls,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.9">1 Pet. i. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.2.7">Rom. ii. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.20">Rev. iii. 20</reference>. The crown of glory will make amends for all; and a believing regard to that will enable us to choose rather to die at a stake with the persecuted, than to live in a palace with the persecutors. <div eID="gen23567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23568" type="x-p"/> V. He foretels the preaching of the gospel in all the world (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.14">v. 14</reference>); <hi type="italic">This gospel shall be preached, and then shall the end come.</hi> Observe here, 1. It is called <hi type="italic">the gospel of the kingdom,</hi> because it reveals the kingdom of grace, which leads to the kingdom of glory; sets up Christ's kingdom in this world; and secures ours in the other world. 2. This gospel, sooner or later, is to be preached in all the world, to every creature, and all nations are to be discipled by it; for in it Christ is to be <hi type="italic">Salvation to the ends of the earth;</hi> for this end the gift of tongues was <hi type="italic">the first-fruits of the Spirit.</hi> 3. The gospel is preached <hi type="italic">for a witness to all nations,</hi> that is, a faithful declaration of the mind and will of God concerning the duty which God requires from man, and the recompence which man may expect from God. It is a <hi type="italic">record</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.5.11">1 John v. 11</reference>), it is a <hi type="italic">witness,</hi> for those who believe, that they shall be saved, and against those who persist in unbelief, that they shall be damned. See <reference osisRef="Mark.16.16">Mark xvi. 16</reference>. But how does this come in here? <div eID="gen23568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23569" type="x-p"/> (1.) It is intimated that the gospel should be, if not heard, yet at least heard of, throughout the then known world, before the destruction of Jerusalem; that the Old-Testament church should not be quite dissolved till the New Testament was pretty well settled, had got considerable footing, and began to make some figure. Better is the face of a corrupt degenerate church than none at all. Within forty years after Christ's death, the <hi type="italic">sound</hi> of the gospel was <hi type="italic">gone forth to the ends of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.10.18">Rom. x. 18</reference>. St. Paul <hi type="italic">fully preached the gospel from Jerusalem, and round about unto Illyricum;</hi> and the other apostles were not idle. The persecuting of the saints at Jerusalem helped to disperse them, so that they <hi type="italic">went every where, preaching the word,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.8.1-Acts.8.4">Acts viii. 1-4</reference>. And when the tidings of the Redeemer are sent over all parts of the world, then shall come the end of the Jewish state. Thus, that which they thought to prevent, by putting Christ to death, they thereby procured; all men <hi type="italic">believed on him, and the Romans came, and took away their place and nation,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.11.48">John xi. 48</reference>. Paul speaks of the gospel being <hi type="italic">come to all the world, and preached to every creature,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.6-Col.1.23">Col. i. 6-23</reference>. <div eID="gen23569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23570" type="x-p"/> (2.) It is likewise intimated that even in times of temptation, trouble, and persecution, the gospel of the kingdom shall be preached and propagated, and shall force its way through the greatest opposition. Though the enemies of the church grow very <hi type="italic">hot,</hi> and many of her friends very <hi type="italic">cool,</hi> yet the gospel shall be preached. And even <hi type="italic">then,</hi> when many fall by the sword and by flame, and many do wickedly, and are corrupted by flatteries, yet then the people that do know their God, shall be strengthened to do the greatest exploits of all, in instructing many; see <reference osisRef="Dan.11.32-Dan.11.33">Dan. xi. 32, 33</reference>; and see an instance, <reference osisRef="Phil.1.12-Phil.1.14">Phil. i. 12-14</reference>. <div eID="gen23570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23571" type="x-p"/> (3.) That which seems chiefly intended here, is, that the end of the world shall be <hi type="italic">then,</hi> and not till then, when the gospel has done its work in the world. The gospel shall be preached, and that work carried on, when you are dead; so that all nations, first or last, shall have either the enjoyment, or the refusal, of the gospel; and <hi type="italic">then cometh the end,</hi> when the kingdom <hi type="italic">shall be delivered up to God, even the Father;</hi> when the mystery of God shall be finished, the mystical body completed, and the nations either converted and saved, or convicted and silenced, by the gospel; <hi type="italic">then shall the end come,</hi> of which he had said before (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.6-Matt.24.7">v. 6, 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">not yet,</hi> not till those intermediate counsels be fulfilled. The world shall stand as long as any of God's chosen ones remain uncalled; but, when they are all gathered in, it will be set on fire immediately. <div eID="gen23571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23572" type="x-p"/> VI. He foretels more particularly the ruin that was coming upon the people of the Jews, their city, temple, and nation, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.15">v. 15</reference>, &c. Here he comes more closely to answer their questions concerning the desolation of the temple; and what he said here, would be of use to his disciples, both for their conduct and for their comfort, in reference to that great event; he describes the several steps of that calamity, such as are usual in war. <div eID="gen23572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23573" type="x-p"/> 1. The Romans <hi type="italic">setting up the abomination of desolation in the holy place,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.15">v. 15</reference>. Now, (1.) Some understand by this an image, or statue, set up in the temple by some of the Roman governors, which was very offensive to the Jews, provoked them to rebel, and so brought the desolation upon them. The image of Jupiter Olympius, which Antiochus caused to be set upon the altar of God, is called <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Bdelygma eremoseos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">The abomination of desolation,</hi> the very word here used by the historian, <reference osisRef="1Macc.1.54">1 Mac. i. 54</reference>. Since the captivity in Babylon, nothing was, nor could be, more distasteful to the Jews than an image in the holy place, as appeared by the mighty opposition they made when Caligula offered to set up his statue there, which had been of fatal consequence, if it had not been prevented, and the matter accommodated, by the conduct of Petronius; but Herod did set up an eagle over the temple-gate; and, some say, the statue of Titus was set up in the temple. (2.) Others choose to expound it by the parallel place (<reference osisRef="Luke.21.20">Luke xxi. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">when ye shall see Jerusalem compassed with armies.</hi> Jerusalem was the holy city, Canaan the holy land, the Mount Moriah, which lay about Jerusalem, for its nearness to the temple was, they thought in a particular manner holy ground; on the country lying round about Jerusalem the Roman army was encamped, that was the abomination that made desolate. The land of an enemy is said to be <hi type="italic">the land which thou abhorrest</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.16">Isa. vii. 16</reference>); so an enemy's army to a weak but wilful people may well be called <hi type="italic">the abomination.</hi> Now this is said to be <hi type="italic">spoken of by Daniel, the prophet,</hi> who spoke more plainly of the Messiah and his kingdom than any of the Old-Testament prophets did. He speaks of an abomination making desolate, which should be set up by Antiochus (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.31">Dan. xi. 31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.11">xii. 11</reference>); but this that our Saviour refers to, we have in the message that the angel brought him (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Dan. ix. 27</reference>), of what should come at the end of seventy weeks, long after the former; <hi type="italic">for the overspreading of abominations,</hi> or, as the margin reads it, <hi type="italic">with the abominable armies</hi> (which comes home to the prophecy here), <hi type="italic">he shall make it desolate.</hi> Armies of idolaters may well be called <hi type="italic">abominable armies;</hi> and some think, the tumults, insurrections, and abominable factions and seditions, in the city and temple, may at least be taken in as part of the abomination making desolate. Christ refers them to that prophecy of Daniel, that they might see how the ruin of their city and temple was spoken of in the Old Testament, which would both confirm his prediction, and take off the odium of it. They might likewise from thence gather the time of it—soon after the cutting off of Messiah the prince; the sin that procured it—their rejecting him, and the certainty of it—<hi type="italic">it is a desolation determined.</hi> As Christ by his precepts confirmed the law, so by his predictions he confirmed the prophecies of the Old Testament, and it will be of good use to compare both together. <div eID="gen23573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23574" type="x-p"/> Reference being here had to a prophecy, which is commonly dark and obscure, Christ inserts this memorandum, "<hi type="italic">Whoso readeth, let him understand;</hi> whoso readeth the prophecy of Daniel, let him understand that it is to have its accomplishment now shortly in the desolations of Jerusalem." Note, Those that read the scriptures, should labour to understand the scriptures, else their reading is to little purpose; we cannot use that which we do not understand. See <reference osisRef="John.5.39">John v. 39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.8.30">Acts viii. 30</reference>. The angel that delivered this prophecy to Daniel, stirred him up to <hi type="italic">know and understand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.9.25">Dan. ix. 25</reference>. And we must not despair of understanding even dark prophecies; the great New-Testament prophecy is called a <hi type="italic">revelation,</hi> not a <hi type="italic">secret.</hi> Now <hi type="italic">things revealed belong to us,</hi> and therefore must be humbly and diligently searched into. Or, <hi type="italic">Let him understand,</hi> not only the scriptures which speak of those things, but by the scriptures let him <hi type="italic">understand the times,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.32">1 Chron. xii. 32</reference>. Let him observe, and take notice; so some read it; let him be assured, that, notwithstanding the vain hopes with which the deluded people feed themselves, the abominable armies will make desolate. <div eID="gen23574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23575" type="x-p"/> 2. The means of preservation which thinking men should betake themselves to (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.16">v. 16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.20">20</reference>); <hi type="italic">Then let them which are in Judea, flee.</hi> Then conclude there is no other way to help yourselves than by flying for the same. We may take this, <div eID="gen23575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23576" type="x-p"/> (1.) As a prediction of the ruin itself; that it should be irresistible; that it would be impossible for the stoutest hearts to make head against it, or contend with it, but they must have recourse to the last shift, getting out of the way. It bespeaks that which Jeremiah so much insisted upon, but in vain, when Jerusalem was besieged by the Chaldeans, that it would be to no purpose to resist, but that it was their wisdom to yield and capitulate; so Christ here, to show how fruitless it would be to stand it out, bids every one make the best of his way. <div eID="gen23576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23577" type="x-p"/> (2.) We may take it as a direction to the followers of Christ what to do, not to <hi type="italic">say, A confederacy</hi> with those who fought and warred against the Romans for the preservation of their city and nation, only that they might consume the wealth of both upon their lusts (for to this very affair, the struggles of the Jews against the Roman power, some years before their final overthrow, the apostle refers, <reference osisRef="Jas.4.1-Jas.4.3">Jam. iv. 1-3</reference>); but let them acquiesce in the decree that was gone forth, and with all speed quit the city and country, as they would quit a falling house or a sinking ship, as Lot quitted Sodom, and Israel the tents of Dathan and Abiram; he shows them, <div eID="gen23577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23578" type="x-p"/> [1.] Whither they must flee—from Judea <hi type="italic">to the mountains;</hi> not the mountains round about Jerusalem, but those in the remote corners of the land, which would be some shelter to them, not so much by their strength as by their secrecy. Israel is said to be <hi type="italic">scattered upon the mountains</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.18.16">2 Chron. xviii. 16</reference>); and see <reference osisRef="Heb.11.38">Heb. xi. 38</reference>. It would be safer among the lions' dens, and the mountains of the leopards, than among the seditious Jews or the enraged Romans. Note, In times of imminent peril and danger, it is not only lawful, but our duty, to seek our own preservation by all good and honest means; and if God opens a door of escape, we ought to make our escape, otherwise we do not trust God but tempt him. There may be a time when even <hi type="italic">those that are in Judea,</hi> where God is known, and his name is great, must <hi type="italic">flee to the mountains;</hi> and while we only go out of the way of danger, not out of the way of duty, we may trust God to provide <hi type="italic">a dwelling for his outcasts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.16.4-Isa.16.5">Isa. xvi. 4, 5</reference>. In times of public calamity, when it is manifest that we cannot be serviceable at home and may be safe abroad, Providence calls us to make our escape. He that flees, may fight again. <div eID="gen23578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23579" type="x-p"/> [2.] What haste they must make, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.17-Matt.24.18">v. 17, 18</reference>. The life will be in danger, in imminent danger, the scourge will slay suddenly; and therefore he <hi type="italic">that is on the house-top,</hi> when the alarm comes, let him not <hi type="italic">come down into the house,</hi> to look after his effects there, but go the nearest way down, to make his escape; and so he that shall be <hi type="italic">in the field,</hi> will find it his wisest course to run immediately, and not return to fetch his clothes or the wealth of his house, for two reasons, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Because the time which would be taken up in packing up his things, would delay his flight. Note, When death is at the door, delays are dangerous; it was the charge to Lot, <hi type="italic">Look not behind thee.</hi> Those that are convinced of the misery of a sinful state, and the ruin that attends them in that state, and, consequently, of the necessity of their fleeing to Christ, must take heed, lest, after all these convictions, they perish eternally by delays. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Because the carrying of his clothes, and his other movables and valuables with him, would but burthen him, and clog his flight. The Syrians, in their flight, <hi type="italic">cast away their garments,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.7.15">2 Kings vii. 15</reference>. At such a time, we must be thankful <hi type="italic">if our lives be given us for a prey,</hi> though we can save nothing, <reference osisRef="Jer.45.4-Jer.45.5">Jer. xlv. 4, 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">For the life is more than meat,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.6.25">ch. vi. 25</reference>. Those who carried off least, were safest in their flight. <hi type="italic">Cantabit vacuus coram latrone viator—The pennyless traveller can lose nothing by robbers.</hi> It was to his own disciples that Christ recommended this forgetfulness of their house and clothes, who had a habitation in heaven, treasure there, and durable clothing, which the enemy could not plunder them of. <hi type="italic">Omnia mea mecum porto—I have all my property with me,</hi> said Bias the philosopher in his flight, empty-handed. He that has grace in his heart carries his all along with him, when tripped of all. <div eID="gen23579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23580" type="x-p"/> Now those to whom Christ said this immediately, did not live to see this dismal day, none of all the twelve but John only; they needed not to be hidden in the mountains (Christ hid them in heaven), but they left the direction to their successors in profession, who pursued it, and it was of use to them; for when the Christians in Jerusalem and Judea saw the ruin coming on, they all retired to a town called <hi type="italic">Pella,</hi> on the other side Jordan, where they were safe; so that of the many thousands that perished in the destruction of Jerusalem, there was not so much as one Christian. See <hi type="italic">Euseb. Eccl. Hist.</hi> lib. 3, cap. 5. Thus <hi type="italic">the prudent man foresees the evil, and hides himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.22.3">Prov. xxii. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.7">Heb. xi. 7</reference>. This warning was not kept private. St. Matthew's gospel was published long before that destruction, so that others might have taken the advantage of it; but their perishing through their unbelief of this, was a figure of their eternal perishing through their unbelief of the warnings Christ gave concerning the wrath to come. <div eID="gen23580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23581" type="x-p"/> [3.] Whom it would go hard with at that time (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.19">v. 19</reference>); <hi type="italic">Woe to them that are with child, and to them that give suck.</hi> To this same event that saying of Christ at his death refers (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.29">Luke xxiii. 29</reference>), They shall say, <hi type="italic">Blessed are the wombs that never bare, and the paps that never gave suck.</hi> Happy are they that have no children to see the murder of; but most unhappy they whose wombs are then bearing, their paps then giving suck: they of all others will be in the most melancholy circumstances. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> To them the famine would be most grievous, when they should see the <hi type="italic">tongue of the sucking child cleaving to the roof of his mouth for thirst,</hi> and themselves by the calamity made more cruel than the sea monsters, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.3-Lam.4.4">Lam. iv. 3, 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> To them the sword would be most terrible, when in the hand of worse than brutal rage. It is a direful midwifery, when the women with child come to be ripped up by the enraged conqueror (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.16">2 Kings xv. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.13.16">Hos. xiii. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.1.13">Amos i. 13</reference>), or the children <hi type="italic">brought forth to their murderer,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.9.13">Hos. ix. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> To them also the flight would be most afflictive,; the women with child cannot make haste, or go far; the sucking child cannot be left behind, or, if it should, <hi type="italic">can a woman forget it, that she should not have compassion on it?</hi> If it be carried along, it retards the mother's flight, and so exposes her life, and is in danger of Mephibosheth's fate, who was lamed by a fall he got in his nurse's flight. <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.4">2 Sam. iv. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen23581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23582" type="x-p"/> [4.] What they should pray against at that time—<hi type="italic">that your flight be not in the winter, nor on the sabbath day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.20">v. 20</reference>. Observe, in general, it becomes Christ's disciples, in times of public trouble and calamity, to be much in prayer; that is a salve for every sore, never out of season, but in a special manner seasonable when we are distressed on every side. There is no remedy but you must flee, the decree is gone forth, so that God will not be entreated to take away his wrath, no, not if <hi type="italic">Noah, Daniel, and Job, stood before him. Let it suffice thee, speak no more of that matter,</hi> but labour to make the best of that which is; and when you cannot in faith pray that you may not be forced to flee, yet pray that the circumstances of it may be graciously ordered, that, though the cup may not pass from you, yet the extremity of the judgment may be prevented. Note, God has the disposing of the circumstances of events, which sometimes make a great alteration one way or other; and therefore in those our eyes must be ever toward him. Christ's bidding them pray for this favour, intimates his purpose of granting it to them; and in a general calamity we must not overlook a circumstantial kindness, but see and own wherein it might have been worse. Christ still bids his disciples to pray for themselves and their friends, that, whenever they were forced to flee, it might be in the most convenient time. Note, When trouble is in prospect, at a great distance, it is good to lay in a stock of prayers beforehand; they must pray, <hi type="italic">First, That their flight,</hi> if it were the will of God, <hi type="italic">might not be in the winter,</hi> when the days are short, the weather cold, the ways dirty, and therefore travelling very uncomfortable, especially for whole families. Paul hastens Timothy to come to him before winter, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.21">2 Tim. iv. 21</reference>. Note, Though the ease of the body is not to be <hi type="italic">mainly</hi> consulted, it ought to be <hi type="italic">duly</hi> considered; though we must take what God sends, and when he sends it, yet we may pray against bodily inconveniences, and are encouraged to do so, in that <hi type="italic">the Lord is for the body. Secondly,</hi> That it might not be <hi type="italic">on the sabbath day;</hi> not on the Jewish sabbath, because travelling then would give offence to them who were angry with the disciples for plucking the ears of corn on the day; not on the Christian sabbath, because being forced to travel on the day would be a grief to themselves. This intimates Christ's design, that a weekly sabbath should be observed in his church after the preaching of the gospel to all the world. We read not of any of the ordinances of the Jewish church, which were purely ceremonial, that Christ ever expressed any care about, because they were all to vanish; but for the sabbath he often showed a concern. It intimates likewise that the sabbath is ordinarily to be observed as a day of rest from travel and worldly labour; but that, according to his own explication of the fourth commandment, works of necessity were lawful on the sabbath day, as this of fleeing from an enemy to save our lives: had it not been lawful, he would have said, "Whatever becomes of you, do not flee on the sabbath day, but abide by it, though you die by it." For we must not commit the least sin, to escape the greatest trouble. But it intimates, likewise, that it is very uneasy and uncomfortable to a good man, to be taken off by any work of necessity from the solemn service and worship of God on the sabbath day. We should pray that we may have quiet undisturbed sabbaths, and may have no other work than sabbath work to do on sabbath days; that we may attend upon the Lord without distraction. It was desirable, that, if they must flee, they might have the benefit and comfort of one sabbath more to help to bear their charges. To flee in the winter is uncomfortable to the body; but to flee on the sabbath day is so to the soul, and the more so when it remembers former sabbaths, as <reference osisRef="Ps.42.4">Ps. xlii. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen23582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23583" type="x-p"/> 3. The greatness of the troubles which should immediately ensue (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.21">v. 21</reference>); <hi type="italic">Then shall be great tribulation;</hi> then when the measure of iniquity is full; then when the servants of God are sealed and secured, then come the troubles; nothing can be done against Sodom till Lot is entered into Zoar, and then look for fire and brimstone immediately. <hi type="italic">There shall be great tribulation.</hi> Great, indeed, when within the city plague and famine raged, and (worse than either) faction and division, so that every man's sword was against his fellow; then and there it was that the hands of the pitiful women flayed their own children. Without the city was the Roman army ready to swallow them up, with a particular rage against them, not only as Jews, but as rebellious Jews. War was the only one of the three sore judgments that David excepted against; but that was it by which the Jews were ruined; and there were famine and pestilence in extremity besides. Josephus's <hi type="italic">History of the Wars of the Jews,</hi> has in it more tragical passages than perhaps any history whatsoever. <div eID="gen23583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23584" type="x-p"/> (1.) It was a desolation unparalleled, such as <hi type="italic">was not since the beginning of the world, nor ever shall be.</hi> Many a city and kingdom has been made desolate, but never any with a desolation like this. Let not daring sinners think that God has done his worst, he can heat the furnace seven times and yet seven times hotter, and will, when he sees greater and still greater abominations. The Romans, when they destroyed Jerusalem, were degenerated from the honour and virtue of their ancestors, which had made even their victories easy to the vanquished.
