And the wilfulness and obstinacy of the Jews themselves contributed much to the increase of the tribulation. No wonder that the ruin of Jerusalem was an unparalleled ruin, when the sin of Jerusalem was an unparalleled sin—even their crucifying Christ. The nearer any people are to God in profession and privileges, the greater and heavier will his judgments be upon them, if they abuse those privileges, and be false to that profession, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.2">Amos iii. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen23584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23585" type="x-p"/> (2.) It was a desolation which, if it should continue long, would be intolerable, so that <hi type="italic">no flesh should be saved,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.22">v. 22</reference>. So triumphantly would death ride, in so many dismal shapes, and with such attendants, that there would be no escaping, but, first or last, all would be cut off. He that escaped one sword, would fall by another, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.17-Isa.24.18">Isa. xxiv. 17, 18</reference>. The computation which Josephus makes of those that were slain in several places, amounts to above two millions. <hi type="italic">No flesh shall be saved;</hi> he doth not say, "No <hi type="italic">soul</hi> shall be saved," for the destruction of the flesh may be for <hi type="italic">the saving of the spirit in the day of the Lord Jesus;</hi> but temporal lives will be sacrificed so profusely, that one would think, if it last awhile, it would make a full end. <div eID="gen23585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23586" type="x-p"/> But here is one word of comfort in the midst of all this terror—that <hi type="italic">for the elects' sake these days shall be shortened,</hi> not made shorter than what God had determined (for <hi type="italic">that which is determined, shall be poured upon the desolate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Dan. ix. 27</reference>), but shorter than what he might have decreed, if he had dealt with them according to their sins; shorter than what the enemy designed, who would have cut all off, if God who made use of them to serve his own purpose, had not set bounds to their wrath; shorter than one who judged by human probabilities would have imagined. Note, [1.] In times of common calamity God manifests his favour to the elect remnant; his jewels, which he will then make up; his peculiar treasure, which he will secure when the lumber is abandoned to the spoiler. [2.] The shortening of calamities is a kindness God often grants for the elects' sake. Instead of complaining that our afflictions last so long, if we consider our defects, we shall see reason to be thankful that they do not last always; when it is bad with us, it becomes us to say, "Blessed be God that it is no worse; blessed be God that it is not hell, endless and remediless misery." It was a lamenting church that said, <hi type="italic">It is of the Lord's mercies that we are not consumed;</hi> and it is for the sake of the elect, lest their spirit should fail before them, if he should contend for ever, and lest they should be tempted to put forth, if not their heart, yet their hand, to iniquity. <div eID="gen23586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23587" type="x-p"/> And now comes in the repeated caution, which was opened before, to take heed of being ensnared by false Christs, and false prophets; (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.23">v. 23</reference>, &c.), who would promise them deliverance, as the lying prophets in Jeremiah's time (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.13">Jer. xiv. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.16-Jer.23.17">xxiii. 16, 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.27.16">xxvii. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.28.2">xxviii. 2</reference>), but would delude them. Times of great trouble are times of great temptation, and therefore we have need to double our guard then. If they shall say, <hi type="italic">Here is a Christ, or there is one,</hi> that shall deliver us from the Romans, do not heed them, it is all but talk; such a deliverance is not to be expected, and therefore not such a deliverer. <div eID="gen23587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23588" type="x-p"/> VII. He foretels the sudden spreading of the gospel in the world, about the time of these great events (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.27-Matt.24.28">v. 27, 28</reference>); <hi type="italic">As the lightning comes out of the east, so shall the coming of the Son of man be.</hi> It comes in here as an antidote against the poison of those seducers, that said, <hi type="italic">Lo, here is Christ,</hi> or, <hi type="italic">Lo, he is there;</hi> compare <reference osisRef="Luke.17.23-Luke.17.24">Luke xvii. 23, 24</reference>. Hearken not to them, for the coming of the Son of man will be as the lightning. <div eID="gen23588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23589" type="x-p"/> 1. It seems primarily to be meant of his coming to set up his spiritual kingdom in the world; where the gospel came in its light and power, there the Son of man came, and in a way quite contrary to the fashion of the seducers and false Christs, who came creeping <hi type="italic">in the desert,</hi> or the <hi type="italic">secret chambers</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.6">2 Tim. iii. 6</reference>); whereas Christ comes not with such a <hi type="italic">spirit of fear,</hi> but <hi type="italic">of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.</hi> The gospel would be remarkable for two things. <div eID="gen23589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23590" type="x-p"/> (1.) Its swift spreading; it shall fly as the lightning; so shall the gospel be preached and propagated. The gospel is light (<reference osisRef="John.3.19">John iii. 19</reference>); and it is not in this as the lightning, that it is a sudden flash, and away, for it is sun-light, and day-light; but it is as lightning in these respects: <div eID="gen23590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23591" type="x-p"/> [1.] It is light from heaven, as the lightning. It is God, and not man, that sends the lightnings, and summons them, that they may go, and say, <hi type="italic">Here we are,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.38.35">Job xxxviii. 35</reference>. It is God that directs it (<reference osisRef="Job.37.3">Job xxxvii. 3</reference>); to man it is one of nature's miracles, above his power to effect, and of nature's mysteries, above his skill to account for: but it is from above; <hi type="italic">his lightnings enlightened the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.97.4">Ps. xcvii. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen23591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23592" type="x-p"/> [2.] It is visible and conspicuous as the lightning. The seducers carried on their depths of Satan in the desert and the secret chambers, shunning the light; heretics were called <hi type="italic">lucifugæ—light-shunners.</hi> But truth seeks no corners, however it may sometimes be forced into them, as the <hi type="italic">woman in the wilderness,</hi> though <hi type="italic">clothed with the sun,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.12.1">Rev. xii. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.12.6">6</reference>. Christ preached his gospel openly (<reference osisRef="John.18.20">John xviii. 20</reference>), and his apostles on <hi type="italic">the housetop</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.27">ch. x. 27</reference>), not <hi type="italic">in a corner,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.26.26">Acts xxvi. 26</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Ps.98.2">Ps. xcviii. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen23592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23593" type="x-p"/> [3.] It was sudden and surprising to the world as the lightning; the Jews indeed had predictions of it, but to the Gentiles it was altogether unlooked for, and came upon them with unaccountable energy, or ever they were aware. It was <hi type="italic">light out of darkness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.4.16">ch. iv. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">2 Cor. iv. 6</reference>. We read of the discomfiting of armies by lightning, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.15">2 Sam. xxii. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.144.6">Ps. cxliv. 6</reference>. The powers of darkness were dispersed and vanquished by the gospel lightning. <div eID="gen23593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23594" type="x-p"/> [4.] It spread far and wide, and that quickly and irresistibly, like the lightning, which comes, suppose, out of the east (Christ is said to ascend <hi type="italic">from the east,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.7.2">Rev. vii. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.2">Isa. xli. 2</reference>), and lighteneth to the west. The propagating of Christianity to so many distant countries, of divers languages, by such unlikely instruments, destitute of all secular advantages, and in the face of so much opposition, and this in so short a time, was one of the greatest miracles that was ever wrought for the confirmation of it; here was Christ upon his white horse, denoting speed as well as strength, and <hi type="italic">going on conquering and to conquer,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.6.2">Rev. vi. 2</reference>. Gospel light rose with the sun, and went with the same, so that the beams of it reached to the ends of the earth, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.18">Rom. x. 18</reference>. Compare with <reference osisRef="Ps.19.3-Ps.19.4">Ps. xix. 3, 4</reference>. Though it was fought against, it could never be cooped up in a desert, or in a secret place, as the seducers were; but by this, according to Gamaliel's rule, proved itself to be <hi type="italic">of God,</hi> that it <hi type="italic">could not be overthrown,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.5.38-Acts.5.39">Acts v. 38, 39</reference>. Christ speaks of <hi type="italic">shining into the west,</hi> because it spread most effectually into those countries which lay west from Jerusalem, as Mr. Herbert observes in his <hi type="italic">Church-militant.</hi> How soon did the gospel lightning reach this island of Great Britain! Tertullian, who wrote in the second century, takes notice of it, <hi type="italic">Britannorum in accessa Romanis loca, Christo tamen subdita—The fastnesses of Britain, though inaccessible to the Romans, were occupied by Jesus Christ.</hi> This was the Lord's doing. <div eID="gen23594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23595" type="x-p"/> (2.) Another thing remarkable concerning the gospel, was, its strange success in those places to which is was spread; it gathered in multitudes, not by external compulsion, but as it were by such a natural instinct and inclination, as brings the birds of prey to their prey; for <hi type="italic">wheresoever the carcase is, there will the eagles be gathered together</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.28">v. 28</reference>), where Christ is preached, souls will be gathered in to him. The <hi type="italic">lifting up of Christ from the earth,</hi> that is, the preaching of Christ crucified, which, one would think, should drive all men from him, will <hi type="italic">draw all men to him</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.12.32">John xii. 32</reference>), according to Jacob's prophecy, that <hi type="italic">to him shall the gathering of the people be,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen. xlix. 10</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Isa.60.8">Isa. lx. 8</reference>. The eagles will be where the carcase is, for it is food for them, it is a feast for them; <hi type="italic">where the slain are, there is she,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.39.30">Job xxxix. 30</reference>. Eagles are said to have a strange sagacity and quickness of scent to find out the prey, and they fly swiftly to it, <reference osisRef="Job.9.26">Job ix. 26</reference>. So those whose spirits God shall stir up, will be effectually drawn to Jesus Christ, to feed upon him; whither should the eagle go but to the prey? Whither should the soul go but to Jesus Christ, who <hi type="italic">has the words of eternal life?</hi> The eagles will distinguish what is proper for them from that which is not; so those who have spiritual senses exercised, will know the voice of the good Shepherd from that of a thief and a robber. Saints will be where the true Christ is, not the false Christs. This is applicable to the desires that are wrought in every gracious soul after Christ, and communion with him. Where he is in his ordinances, there will his servants choose to be. A living principle of grace is a kind of natural instinct in all the saints, drawing them to Christ to live upon him. <div eID="gen23595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23596" type="x-p"/> 2. Some understand <reference osisRef="Matt.24.29-Matt.24.31">these verses</reference> of the coming of the Son of man <hi type="italic">to destroy Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.3.1-Mal.3.2">Mal. iii. 1, 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mal.3.5">5</reference>. So much was there of an extraordinary display of divine power and justice in that event, that it is called <hi type="italic">the coming of Christ.</hi> <div eID="gen23596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23597" type="x-p"/> Now here are two things intimated concerning it. <div eID="gen23597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23598" type="x-p"/> (1.) That to the most it would be as unexpected as a flash of lightning, which indeed gives warning of the clap of thunder which follows, but is itself surprising. The seducers say, <hi type="italic">Lo, here is Christ</hi> to deliver us; or there is one, a creature of their own fancies; but ere they are aware, the wrath of the Lamb, the true Christ, will arrest them, and they shall not escape. <div eID="gen23598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23599" type="x-p"/> (2.) That it might be as justly expected as that the eagle should fly to the carcases; though they put far from them the evil day, yet the desolation will come as certainly as the birds of prey to a dead carcase, that lies exposed in the open field. [1.] The Jews were so corrupt and degenerate, so vile and vicious, that they were become a carcase, obnoxious to the righteous judgment of God; they were also so factious and seditious, and every way so provoking to the Romans, that they had made themselves obnoxious to their resentments, and an inviting prey to them. [2.] The Romans were as an eagle, and the ensign of their armies was an eagle. The army of the Chaldeans is said <hi type="italic">to fly as the eagle that hasteth to eat,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.1.8">Hab. i. 8</reference>. The ruin of the New-Testament Babylon is represented by a call to the birds of prey to come and feast upon the slain, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.17-Rev.19.18">Rev. xix. 17, 18</reference>. Notorious malefactors have their eyes eaten out by <hi type="italic">the young eagles</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.17">Prov. xxx. 17</reference>); the Jews were hung up in chains, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.33">Jer. vii. 33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.16.4">xvi. 4</reference>. [3.] The Jews can no more preserve themselves from the Romans than the carcase can secure itself from the eagles. [4.] The destruction shall find out the Jews wherever they are, as the eagle scents the prey. Note, When a people do by their sin make themselves carcases, putrid and loathsome, nothing can be expected but that God should send eagles among them, to devour and destroy them. <div eID="gen23599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23600" type="x-p"/> 3. It is very applicable to the day of judgment, the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ in that day, and <hi type="italic">our gathering together unto him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.1">2 Thess. ii. 1</reference>. Now see here, <div eID="gen23600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23601" type="x-p"/> (1.) How he shall come; <hi type="italic">as the lightning,</hi> The time was now at hand, when he should <hi type="italic">depart out of the world, to go to the Father.</hi> Therefore those that enquire after Christ must not go into the desert or the secret place, nor listen to every one that will put up the finger to invite them to a sight of Christ; but let them look upward, for the heavens must contain him, and thence <hi type="italic">we look for the Saviour</hi> (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">Phil. iii. 20</reference>); he shall <hi type="italic">come in the clouds,</hi> as the lightning doth, and <hi type="italic">every eye shall see him,</hi> as they say it is natural for all living creatures to turn their faces towards the lightning, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.7">Rev. i. 7</reference>. Christ will appear to all the world, from one end of heaven to the other; nor shall any thing be hid from the light and heat of that day. <div eID="gen23601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23602" type="x-p"/> (2.) How the saints shall be gathered to him; as the eagles are to the carcase by natural instinct, and with the greatest swiftness and alacrity imaginable. Saints, when they shall be fetched to glory, will be carried as on eagles' wings (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.4">Exod. xix. 4</reference>), as on angels' wings. <hi type="italic">They shall mount up with wings, like eagles,</hi> and like them renew their youth. <div eID="gen23602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23603" type="x-p"/> VIII. He foretels his second coming at the <hi type="italic">end of time,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.29-Matt.24.31">v. 29-31</reference>. <hi type="italic">The sun shall be darkened,</hi> &c. <div eID="gen23603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23604" type="x-p"/> 1. Some think this is to be understood only of the destruction of Jerusalem and the Jewish nation; the darkening of the sun, moon, and stars, denotes the eclipse of the glory of that state, its convulsions, and the general confusion that attended that desolation. Great slaughter and devastation are in the Old Testament thus set forth (as <reference osisRef="Isa.13.10">Isa. xiii. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.34.4">xxxiv. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.7">Ezek. xxxii. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.31">Joel ii. 31</reference>); or by the sun, moon, and stars, may be meant the temple, Jerusalem, and the cities of Judah, which should all come to ruin. The <hi type="italic">sign of the Son of man</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.30">v. 30</reference>) means a signal appearance of the power and justice of the Lord Jesus in it, avenging his own blood on them that imprecated the guilt of it upon themselves and their children; and the gathering <hi type="italic">of his elect</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.31">v. 31</reference>) signifies the delivering of a remnant from this sin and ruin. <div eID="gen23604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23605" type="x-p"/> 2. It seems rather to refer to Christ's second coming. The destruction of the particular enemies of the church was typical of the complete conquest of them all; and therefore what will be done really at the great day, may be applied metaphorically to those destructions: but still we must attend to the principal scope of them; and while we are all agreed to expect Christ's second coming, what need is there to put such strained constructions as some do, upon <reference osisRef="Matt.24.29-Matt.24.31">these verses</reference>, which speak of it so clearly, and so agreeably to other scriptures, especially when Christ is here answering an enquiry concerning his coming at the end of the world, which Christ was never shy of speaking of to his disciples? <div eID="gen23605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23606" type="x-p"/> The only objection against this, is, that it is said to be <hi type="italic">immediately after the tribulation of those days;</hi> but as to that, (1.) It is usual in the prophetical style to speak of things great and certain as near and just at hand, only to express the greatness and certainty of them. Enoch spoke of Christ's second coming as within ken, <hi type="italic">Behold, the Lord cometh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.14">Jude 14</reference>. (2.) <hi type="italic">A thousand years are</hi> in God's sight <hi type="italic">but as one day,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.8">2 Pet. iii. 8</reference>. It is there urged, with reference to this very thing, and so it might be said to be immediately after. The tribulation of those days includes not only the destruction of Jerusalem, but all the other tribulations which the church must pass through; not only its share in the calamities of the nations, but the tribulations peculiar to itself; while the nations are torn with wars, and the church with schisms, delusions, and persecutions, we cannot say that the tribulation of those days is over; the whole state of the church on earth is militant, we must count upon that; but when the church's tribulation is over, her warfare accomplished, and what is behind of the sufferings of Christ filled up, then look for the end. <div eID="gen23606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23607" type="x-p"/> Now concerning Christ's second coming, it is here foretold, <div eID="gen23607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23608" type="x-p"/> [1.] That there shall be then a great and amazing change of the creatures, and particularly the <hi type="italic">heavenly bodies</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.29">v. 29</reference>). <hi type="italic">The sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light.</hi> The moon shines with a borrowed light, and therefore if the sun, from whom she borrows her light, is turned into darkness, she must fail of course, and become bankrupt. <hi type="italic">The stars shall fall;</hi> they shall lose their light, and disappear, and be as if they were fallen; and <hi type="italic">the powers of heaven shall be shaken.</hi> This intimates, <div eID="gen23608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23609" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That there shall be a great change, in order to the making of all things new. Then shall be <hi type="italic">the restitution of all things,</hi> when the heavens shall not be cast away as a rag, but <hi type="italic">changed as a vesture,</hi> to be worn in a better fashion, <reference osisRef="Ps.102.26">Ps. cii. 26</reference>. They shall <hi type="italic">pass away with a great noise,</hi> that there may be <hi type="italic">new heavens,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.10-2Pet.3.13">2 Pet. iii. 10-13</reference>. <div eID="gen23609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23610" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It shall be a visible change, and such as all the world must take notice of; for such the darkening of the sun and moon cannot but be: and it would be an amazing change; for the heavenly bodies are not so liable to alteration as the creatures of this lower world are. The days of heaven, and the continuance of the sun and moon, are used to express that which is lasting and unchangeable (As <reference osisRef="Ps.89.29">Ps. lxxxix. 29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.36.37">xxxvi. 37</reference>); yet they shall thus be shaken. <div eID="gen23610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23611" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It shall be a universal change. If the sun be turned into darkness, and the powers of heaven be shaken, the earth cannot but be turned into a dungeon, and its foundation made to tremble. <hi type="italic">Howl, fir trees, if the cedars be shaken.</hi> When the stars of heaven drop, no marvel if the <hi type="italic">everlasting mountains melt,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">perpetual hills bow.</hi> Nature shall sustain a general shock and convulsion, which yet shall be no hindrance to the joy and rejoicing of heaven and earth <hi type="italic">before the Lord, when he cometh to judge the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.96.11">Ps. xcvi. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.96.13">13</reference>); they shall as it were <hi type="italic">glory in the tribulation.</hi> <div eID="gen23611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23612" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> The darkening of the sun, moon, and stars, which were <hi type="italic">made to rule over the day, and over the night</hi> (which is the first dominion we find of any creature, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.16-Gen.1.18">Gen. i. 16-18</reference>), signifies the <hi type="italic">putting down of all rule, authority, and power</hi> (even that which seems of the greatest antiquity and usefulness), <hi type="italic">that the kingdom may be delivered up to God, even the Father,</hi> and he may be <hi type="italic">All in all,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.24">1 Cor. xv. 24</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.28">28</reference>. The sun was darkened at the death of Christ, for then was in one sense <hi type="italic">the judgment of this world</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.12.31">John xii. 31</reference>), an indication of what would be at the general judgment. <div eID="gen23612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23613" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> The glorious appearance of our Lord Jesus, who will then show himself as the <hi type="italic">Brightness of his Father's glory, and the express Image of his person,</hi> will darken the sun and moon, as a candle is darkened in the beams of the noon-day sun; they will have no glory, <hi type="italic">by reason of the glory that excelleth,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.10">2 Cor. iii. 10</reference>. Then <hi type="italic">the sun shall be ashamed, and the moon confounded,</hi> when God shall appear, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.23">Isa. xxiv. 23</reference>. <div eID="gen23613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23614" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Sixthly,</hi> The sun and moon shall be then darkened, because there will be no more occasion for them. To sinners, that choose their portion in this life, all comfort will be eternally denied; as they shall not have a drop of water, so not a ray of light. Now God causeth his sun to rise on the earth, but then <hi type="italic">Interdico tib sole et luna—I forbid thee the light of the sun and the moon.</hi> Darkness must be their portion. To the saints that had their treasure above, such light of joy and comfort will be given as shall supersede that of the sun and moon, and render it useless. What need is there of vessels of light, when we come to <hi type="italic">the Fountain and Father of light</hi>? See <reference osisRef="Isa.60.19">Isa. lx. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.5">Rev. xxii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen23614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23615" type="x-p"/> [2.] That <hi type="italic">then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.30">v. 30</reference>), the Son of man himself, as it follows here, <hi type="italic">They shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds.</hi> At his first coming, he was <hi type="italic">set for a Sign that should be spoken against</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.34">Luke ii. 34</reference>), but at his second coming, a sign that should be admired. Ezekiel was <hi type="italic">a son of man set for a sign,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.6">Ezek. xii. 6</reference>. Some make this a prediction of the harbingers and forerunners of his coming, giving notice of his approach; <hi type="italic">a light shining before him, and the fire devouring</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.3">Ps. l. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.11-1Kgs.19.12">1 Kings xix. 11, 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">the beams coming out of his hand, where had long been the hiding of his power,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.3.4">Hab. iii. 4</reference>. It is a groundless conceit of some of the ancients, that this sign of the Son of man, will be the sign of the cross displayed as a banner. It will certainly be such a clear convincing sign as will dash infidelity quite out of countenance, and fill their faces with shame, who said, <hi type="italic">Where is the promise of his coming?</hi> <div eID="gen23615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23616" type="x-p"/> [3.] That <hi type="italic">then all the tribes of the earth shall mourn,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.30">v. 30</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Rev.1.7">Rev. i. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">All the kindreds of the earth shall then wail because of him;</hi> some of all the tribes and kindreds of the earth shall mourn; for the greater part will tremble at his approach, while the chosen remnant, one of a family and two of a tribe, shall lift up their heads with joy, knowing that their redemption draws nigh, and their Redeemer. Note, Sooner or later, all sinners will be mourners; penitent sinners look to Christ, and mourn after a godly sort; and they who sow in those tears, shall shortly reap in joy; impenitent sinners <hi type="italic">shall look unto him whom they have pierced,</hi> and, though they laugh now, shall mourn and weep after a devilish sort, in endless horror and despair. <div eID="gen23616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23617" type="x-p"/> [4.] That <hi type="italic">then they shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven, with power and great glory.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The judgment of the great day will be committed to the Son of man, both in pursuance and in recompence of his great undertaking for us as Mediator, <reference osisRef="John.5.22">John v. 22</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.27">27</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The Son of man will at that day come in the clouds of heaven. Much of the sensible intercourse between heaven and earth is by the clouds; they are betwixt them, as it were, the <hi type="italic">medium participationis—the medium of participation,</hi> drawn by heaven from the earth, distilled by heaven upon the earth. Christ went to heaven in a cloud, and <hi type="italic">will in like manner come again,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.1.9">Acts i. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.1.11">11</reference>. <hi type="italic">Behold, he cometh in the clouds,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.1.7">Rev. i. 7</reference>. A cloud will be the Judge's chariot (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.3">Ps. civ. 3</reference>), his robe (<reference osisRef="Rev.10.1">Rev. x. 1</reference>), his pavilion (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.11">Ps. xviii. 11</reference>), his throne, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.14">Rev. xiv. 14</reference>. When the world was destroyed by water, the judgment came in the clouds of heaven, for the windows of heaven were opened; so shall it be when it shall be destroyed by fire. Christ went before Israel in a cloud, which had a bright side and a dark side; so will the cloud have in which Christ will come at the great day, it will bring both comfort and terror. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He will <hi type="italic">come with power and great glory:</hi> his first coming was in weakness and great meanness (<reference osisRef="2Cor.13.4">2 Cor. xiii. 4</reference>); but his second coming will be with power and glory, agreeable both to the dignity of his person and to the purposes of his coming. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> He will be seen with bodily eyes in his coming: <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> the Son of man will be the Judge, that he may be seen, that sinners thereby may be the more confounded, who shall see him as Balaam did, <hi type="italic">but not nigh</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.24.17">Num. xxiv. 17</reference>), see him, but not as theirs. It added to the torment of that damned sinner, that <hi type="italic">he saw Abraham afar off.</hi> "Is this he whom we have slighted, and rejected, and rebelled against; whom we have crucified to ourselves afresh; who might have been our Saviour, but is our Judge, and will be our enemy for ever?" <hi type="italic">The Desire of all nations</hi> will then be their dread. <div eID="gen23617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23618" type="x-p"/> [5.] That <hi type="italic">he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.31">v. 31</reference>. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The angels shall be attendants upon Christ at his second coming; they are called <hi type="italic">his</hi> angels, which proves him to be God, and Lord of the angels; they shall be obliged to wait upon him. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> These attendants shall be employed by him as officers of the court in the judgment of that day; they are now ministering spirits sent forth by him (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.14">Heb. i. 14</reference>), and will be so then. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Their ministration will be ushered in with a great sound of a trumpet, to awaken and alarm a sleeping world. This trumpet is spoken of, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.52">1 Cor. xv. 52</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.16">and 1 Thess. iv. 16</reference>. At the giving of the law on mount Sinai, the sound of the trumpet was remarkably terrible (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.13">Exod. xix. 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.16">16</reference>); but much more will it be so in the great day. By the law, trumpets were to be sounded for the calling of assemblies (<reference osisRef="Num.10.2">Num. x. 2</reference>), in praising God (<reference osisRef="Ps.81.3">Ps. lxxxi. 3</reference>), in offering sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Num.10.10">Num. x. 10</reference>), and in proclaiming the year of jubilee, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.9">Lev. xxv. 9</reference>. Very fitly therefore shall there be the sound of a trumpet at the last day, when the general assembly shall be called, when the praises of God shall be gloriously celebrated, when sinners shall fall as sacrifices to divine justice, and when the saints shall enter upon their eternal jubilee. <div eID="gen23618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23619" type="x-p"/> [6.] That <hi type="italic">they shall gather together his elect from the four winds.</hi> Note, At the second coming of Jesus Christ, there will be a general meeting of all the saints. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The <hi type="italic">elect</hi> only will be gathered, the chosen remnant, who are but few in comparison with the many that are only <hi type="italic">called.</hi> This is the foundation of the saints' eternal happiness, that they are God's elect. The gifts of love to eternity follow the thought of love from eternity; and <hi type="italic">the Lord knows them that are his. Secondly,</hi> The angels shall be employed to bring them together, as Christ's servants, and as the saints' friends; we have the commission given them, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.5">Ps. l. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Gather my saints together unto me;</hi> nay, it will be said to them, <hi type="italic">Habetis fratres—These are your brethren;</hi> for the elect will then <hi type="italic">be equal to the angels,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.20.36">Luke xx. 36</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> They <hi type="italic">shall be gathered from one end of heaven to the other;</hi> the elect of God are scattered abroad (<reference osisRef="John.11.52">John xi. 52</reference>), there are some in all places, in all nations (<reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Rev. vii. 9</reference>); but when that great gathering day comes, there shall not one of them be missing; distance of place shall keep none out of heaven, if distance of affection do not. <hi type="italic">Undique ad c&#339;los tantundem est viæ—Heaven is equally accessible from every place.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Matt.8.11">ch. viii. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.6">Isa. xliii. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.12">xlix. 12</reference>.
entries.4a7ef3d414f2d863036f0de77563e19e0e2821ac: <div eID="gen23619" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Parable of the Fig-Tree; Awful Predictions; The Duty of Watchfulness; The Good and Evil Steward.</title> <div sID="gen23620" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">32</hi> Now learn a parable of the fig tree; When his branch is yet tender, and putteth forth leaves, ye know that summer <hi type="italic">is</hi> nigh: <hi type="super">33</hi> So likewise ye, when ye shall see all these things, know that it is near, <hi type="italic">even</hi> at the doors. 34 Verily I say unto you, This generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled. <hi type="super">35</hi> Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away. <hi type="super">36</hi> But of that day and hour knoweth no <hi type="italic">man,</hi> no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only. <hi type="super">37</hi> But as the days of Noe <hi type="italic">were,</hi> so shall also the coming of the Son of man be. <hi type="super">38</hi> For as in the days that were before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day that Noe entered into the ark, <hi type="super">39</hi> And knew not until the flood came, and took them all away; so shall also the coming of the Son of man be. <hi type="super">40</hi> Then shall two be in the field; the one shall be taken, and the other left. <hi type="super">41</hi> Two <hi type="italic">women shall be</hi> grinding at the mill; the one shall be taken, and the other left. 42 Watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come. <hi type="super">43</hi> But know this, that if the goodman of the house had known in what watch the thief would come, he would have watched, and would not have suffered his house to be broken up. <hi type="super">44</hi> Therefore be ye also ready: for in such an hour as ye think not the Son of man cometh. <hi type="super">45</hi> Who then is a faithful and wise servant, whom his lord hath made ruler over his household, to give them meat in due season? <hi type="super">46</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">is</hi> that servant, whom his lord when he cometh shall find so doing. <hi type="super">47</hi> Verily I say unto you, That he shall make him ruler over all his goods. 48 But and if that evil servant shall say in his heart, My lord delayeth his coming; <hi type="super">49</hi> And shall begin to smite <hi type="italic">his</hi> fellow-servants, and to eat and drink with the drunken; 50 The lord of that servant shall come in a day when he looketh not for <hi type="italic">him,</hi> and in an hour that he is not aware of, 51 And shall cut him asunder, and appoint <hi type="italic">him</hi> his portion with the hypocrites: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. <div eID="gen23620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23621" type="x-p"/> We have here the practical application of the foregoing prediction; in general, we must expect and prepare for the events here foretold. <div eID="gen23621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23622" type="x-p"/> I. We must expect them; "<hi type="italic">Now learn a parable of the fig-tree,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.32-Matt.24.33">v. 32, 33</reference>. Now learn what use to make of the things you have heard; so observe and understand the signs of the times, and compare them with the predictions of the word, as from thence to foresee what is at the door, that you may provide accordingly." The parable of the fig-tree is no more than this, that its budding and blossoming are a presage of summer; for as the <hi type="italic">stork</hi> in the heaven, so the trees of the field, <hi type="italic">know their appointed time.</hi> The beginning of the working of second causes assures us of the progress and perfection of it. Thus when God begins to fulfil prophecies, he will make an end. There is a certain series in the works of providence, as there is in the works of nature. The signs of the times are compared with the prognostics of <hi type="italic">the face of the sky</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.3">ch. xvi. 3</reference>), so here with those of <hi type="italic">the face of the earth;</hi> when that is renewed, we foresee that summer is coming, not immediately, but at some distance; after <hi type="italic">the branch grows tender,</hi> we expect the March winds, and the April showers, before the summer comes; however, we are sure it is coming; "so likewise ye, when the gospel day shall dawn, count upon it, that through this variety of events which I have told you of, the perfect day will come. <hi type="italic">The things revealed must shortly come to pass</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.1">Rev. i. 1</reference>); they must come in their own order, in the order appointed for them. <hi type="italic">Know that it is near.</hi>" He does not here say what, but it is that which the hearts of his disciples are upon, and which they are inquisitive after, and long for; <hi type="italic">the kingdom of God is near,</hi> so it is expressed in the parallel place, <reference osisRef="Luke.21.31">Luke xxi. 31</reference>. Note, When the trees of righteousness begin to bud and blossom, when God's people promise faithfulness, it is a happy presage of good times. In them God begins his work, first prepares their heart, and then he will go on with it; for, <hi type="italic">as for God, his work is perfect;</hi> and he will <hi type="italic">revive it in the midst of their years.</hi> <div eID="gen23622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23623" type="x-p"/> Now touching the events foretold here, which we are to expect, <div eID="gen23623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23624" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ here assures us of the certainty of them (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.35">v. 35</reference>); <hi type="italic">Heaven and earth shall pass away;</hi> they continue this day indeed, according to God's ordinance, but they shall not continue for ever (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.25-Ps.102.26">Ps. cii. 25, 26</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.10">2 Pet. iii. 10</reference>); <hi type="italic">but my words shall not pass away.</hi> Note, The word of Christ is more sure and lasting than heaven and earth. <hi type="italic">Hath he spoken? And shall he not do it?</hi> We may build with more assurance upon the word of Christ than we can upon the pillars of heaven, or the strong foundations of the earth; for, when they shall be made to tremble and totter, and shall be no more, the word of Christ shall remain, and be in full force, power, and virtue. See <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.24-1Pet.1.25">1 Pet. i. 24, 25</reference>. <hi type="italic">It is easier for heaven and earth to pass,</hi> than the word of Christ; so it is expressed, <reference osisRef="Luke.16.17">Luke xvi. 17</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.54.10">Isa. liv. 10</reference>. The accomplishment of these prophecies might seem to be delayed, and intervening events might seem to disagree with them, but do not think that therefore the word of Christ is fallen to the ground, for that shall never pass away: though it be not fulfilled, either in the time or in the way that we have prescribed; yet, in God's time, which is the best time, and in God's way, which is the best way, it shall certainly be fulfilled. Every word of Christ is very pure, and therefore very sure. <div eID="gen23624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23625" type="x-p"/> 2. He here instructs us as to the time of them, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.34">v. 34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.36">36</reference>. As to this, it is well observed by the learned Grotius, that there is a manifest distinction made between the <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">tauta</hi></hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.34">v. 34</reference>), and the <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ekeine</hi></hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.36">v. 36</reference>), <hi type="italic">these things,</hi> and <hi type="italic">that day and hour;</hi> which will help to clear this prophecy. <div eID="gen23625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23626" type="x-p"/> (1.) As to <hi type="italic">these things,</hi> the wars, seductions, and persecutions, here foretold, and especially the ruin of the Jewish nation; "<hi type="italic">This generation shall not pass away, till all these things be fulfilled</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.34">v. 34</reference>); there are those now alive, that shall see Jerusalem destroyed, and the Jewish church brought to an end." Because it might seem strange, he backs it with a solemn asseveration; "<hi type="italic">Verily, I say unto you.</hi> You may take my word for it, these things are at the door." Christ often speaks of the nearness of that desolation, the more to affect people, and quicken them to prepare for it. Note, There may be greater trials and troubles yet before us, in our own day, than we are aware of. They that are old, know not what sons of Anak may be reserved for their last encounters. <div eID="gen23626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23627" type="x-p"/> (2.) But as to <hi type="italic">that day and hour</hi> which will put a period to time, <hi type="italic">that knoweth no man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.36">v. 36</reference>. Therefore take heed of confounding these two, as <hi type="italic">they</hi> did, who, from the words of Christ and the apostles; letters, inferred that <hi type="italic">the day of Christ was at hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.2">2 Thess. ii. 2</reference>. No, it was not; <hi type="italic">this generation,</hi> and many another, <hi type="italic">shall pass,</hi> before <hi type="italic">that day and hour</hi> come. Note, [1.] There is a certain day and hour fixed for the judgment to come; it is called <hi type="italic">the day of the Lord,</hi> because so unalterably fixed. None of God's judgments are adjourned <hi type="italic">sine die—without the appointment of a certain day.</hi> [2.] That day and hour are a great secret. <div eID="gen23627" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen23628"/> <l level="1" sID="gen23629"/>Prudens futuri temporis exitum<l eID="gen23629" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen23630"/>Caliginosa nocte premit Deus.<l eID="gen23630" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen23631"/>But Heaven has wisely hid from human sight<l eID="gen23631" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen23632"/>The dark decrees of future fate,<l eID="gen23632" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen23633"/>And sown their seeds in depth of nights. <hi type="small-caps">Horace.</hi><l eID="gen23633" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen23628"/> <div sID="gen23634" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">No man knows it;</hi> not the wisest by their sagacity, not the best by any divine discovery. We all know that there shall be such a day; but none knows when it shall be, no, not the angels; though their capacities for knowledge are great, and their opportunities of knowing this advantageous (they dwell at the fountain-head of light), and though they are to be employed in the solemnity of that day, yet they are not told when it shall be: none <hi type="italic">knows but my Father only.</hi> This is one of those <hi type="italic">secret things</hi> which <hi type="italic">belong to the Lord our God.</hi> The uncertainty of the time of Christ's coming, is, to those who are watchful, <hi type="italic">a savour of life unto life,</hi> and makes them more watchful; but to those who are careless, it is <hi type="italic">a savour of death unto death,</hi> and makes them more careless. <div eID="gen23634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23635" type="x-p"/> II. To this end we must expect these events, that we may prepare for them; and here we have a caution against security and sensuality, which will make it a dismal day indeed to us, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.37-Matt.24.41">v. 37-41</reference>. In these verses we have such an idea given us of the judgment day, as may serve to startle and awaken us, that we may not sleep as others do. <div eID="gen23635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23636" type="x-p"/> It will be a surprising day, and a separating day. <div eID="gen23636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23637" type="x-p"/> 1. It will be a surprising day, as the deluge was to the old world, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.37-Matt.24.39">v. 37-39</reference>. That which he here intends to describe, is, the posture of the world at the coming of the Son of man; besides his first coming, to save, he has other comings to judge. He saith (<reference osisRef="John.9.39">John ix. 39</reference>), <hi type="italic">For judgment I am come;</hi> and for judgment he will come; for all judgment is committed to him, both that of the word, and that of the sword. <div eID="gen23637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23638" type="x-p"/> Now this here is applicable, <div eID="gen23638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23639" type="x-p"/> (1.) To <hi type="italic">temporal judgments,</hi> particularly that which was now hastening upon the nation and people of the Jews; though they had fair warning given them of it, and there were many prodigies that were presages of it, yet it found them secure, crying, <hi type="italic">Peace and safety,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.3">1 Thess. v. 3</reference>. The siege was laid to Jerusalem by Titus Vespasian, when they were met at the passover in the midst of their mirth; like the men of Laish, they dwelt careless when the ruin arrested them, <reference osisRef="Judg.18.7">Judg. xviii. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.18.27">27</reference>. The destruction of Babylon, both that in the Old Testament and that in the New, comes when she saith, <hi type="italic">I shall be a lady for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.47.7-Isa.47.9">Isa. xlvii. 7-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.7">Rev. xviii. 7</reference>. Therefore the plagues come in a moment, in one day. Note, Men's unbelief shall not make God's threatenings of no effect. <div eID="gen23639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23640" type="x-p"/> (2.) To <hi type="italic">the eternal judgment;</hi> so the judgment of the great day is called, <reference osisRef="Heb.6.2">Heb. vi. 2</reference>. Though notice has been given of it from Enoch, yet, when it comes, it will be unlooked for by the most of men; the latter days, which are nearest to that day, will produce scoffers, that say, <hi type="italic">Where is the promise of his coming?</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.3-2Pet.3.4">2 Pet. iii. 3, 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.18.8">Luke xviii. 8</reference>. Thus it will be when the world that now is shall be destroyed by fire; for thus it was when the old world, being overflowed by water, perished, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.6-2Pet.3.7">2 Pet. iii. 6, 7</reference>. Now Christ here shows what were the temper and posture of the old world when the deluge came. <div eID="gen23640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23641" type="x-p"/> [1.] They were sensual and worldly; <hi type="italic">they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage.</hi> It is not said, They were killing and stealing, and whoring and swearing (these were indeed the horrid crimes of some of the worst of them; <hi type="italic">the earth was full of violence</hi>); but they were all of them, except Noah, over head and ears in the world, and regardless of the word of God, and this ruined them. Note, Universal neglect of religion is a more dangerous symptom to any people than particular instances here and there of daring irreligion. <hi type="italic">Eating and drinking</hi> are necessary to the preservation of man's life; <hi type="italic">marrying and giving in marriage</hi> are necessary to the preservation of mankind; but, <hi type="italic">Licitus perimus omnes—These lawful things undo us,</hi> unlawfully managed. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They were unreasonable in it, inordinate and entire in the pursuit of the delights of sense, and the gains of the world; they were wholly taken up with these things, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">esan trogontes</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">they were eating;</hi> they were in these things as in their element, as if they had their being for no other end than <hi type="italic">to eat and drink,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.56.12">Isa. lvi. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They were unreasonable in it; they were entire and intent upon the world and the flesh, when the destruction was at the door, which they had had such fair warning of. They were eating and drinking, when they should have been repenting and praying; when God, by the ministry of Noah, called to <hi type="italic">weeping and mourning, then joy and gladness.</hi> This was to them, as it was to Israel afterwards, the unpardonable sin (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.12">Isa. xxii. 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.14">14</reference>), especially, because it was in defiance of those warnings by which they should have been awakened. "<hi type="italic">Let us eat and drink, for to-morrow we die;</hi> if it must be a short life, let it be a merry one." The apostle James speaks of this as the general practice of the wealthy Jews before the destruction of Jerusalem; when they should have been <hi type="italic">weeping for the miseries that were coming upon them, they were living in pleasure, and nourishing their hearts as in a day of slaughter,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.5.1">Jam. v. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jas.5.5">5</reference>. <div eID="gen23641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23642" type="x-p"/> [2.] They were secure and careless; <hi type="italic">they knew not, until the flood came,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.39">v. 39</reference>. <hi type="italic">Knew not!</hi> Surely they could not but know. Did not God, by Noah, give them fair warning of it? Did he not call them to repentance, while his long-suffering waited? <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.19-1Pet.3.20">1 Pet. iii. 19, 20</reference>. But they knew not, that is, they believed not; they might have known, but would not know. Note, What we know of <hi type="italic">the things that belong to our everlasting peace,</hi> if we do not mix faith with it, and improve it, is all one as if we did not know it at all. Their <hi type="italic">not knowing</hi> is joined with their <hi type="italic">eating, and drinking, and marrying;</hi> for, <hi type="italic">First, Therefore</hi> they were sensual, because they were secure. Note, the reason why people are so eager in the pursuit, and so entangled in the pleasures of this world, is, because they do not know, and believe, and consider, the eternity which they are upon the brink of. Did we know aright that all these things must shortly be dissolved, and we must certainly survive them, we should not set our eyes and hearts so much upon them as we do. <hi type="italic">Secondly, Therefore</hi> they were secure, because they were sensual; <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> they knew not that the flood was coming, because they were eating and drinking; were so taken up with things seen and present, that they had neither time nor heart to mind the things not seen as yet, which they were warned of. Note, As security bolsters men up in their brutal sensuality; so sensuality rocks them asleep in their carnal security. <hi type="italic">They knew not, until the flood came.</hi> 1. The flood did come, though they would not foresee it. Note, Those that will not know by faith, shall be made to know by feeling, <hi type="italic">the wrath of God revealed from heaven against their ungodliness and unrighteousness.</hi> The evil day is never the further off for men's putting it far off from them. 2. They did not know it till it was too late to prevent it, as they might have done if they had known it in time, which made it so much the more grievous. Judgments are most terrible and amazing to the secure, and those that have made a jest of them. <div eID="gen23642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23643" type="x-p"/> The application of this, concerning the old world, we have in these words; <hi type="italic">So shall the coming of the Son of man be;</hi> that is, (1.) In such a posture shall he find people, eating and drinking, and not expecting him. Note, Security and sensuality are likely to be the epidemical diseases of the latter days. All <hi type="italic">slumber and sleep, and at midnight the bridegroom comes.</hi> All are off their watch, and at their ease. (2.) With such a power, and for such a purpose, will he come upon them. As the flood took away the sinners of the old world, irresistibly and irrecoverably; so shall secure sinners, that mocked at Christ and his coming, be taken away by <hi type="italic">the wrath of the Lamb, when the great day of his wrath comes,</hi> which will be like the coming of the deluge, a destruction which there is no fleeing from. <div eID="gen23643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23644" type="x-p"/> 2. It will be a separating day (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.40-Matt.24.41">v. 40, 41</reference>); <hi type="italic">Then shall two be in the field.</hi> Two ways this may be applied. <div eID="gen23644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23645" type="x-p"/> (1.) We may apply it to the success of the gospel, especially at the first preaching of it; it divided the world; <hi type="italic">some believed the things which were spoken,</hi> and were taken to Christ; <hi type="italic">others believed not,</hi> and were left to perish in their unbelief. Those of the same age, place, capacity, employment, and condition, in the world, <hi type="italic">grinding in the same mill,</hi> those of the same family, nay, those that were joined in the same bond of marriage, were, one effectually called, the other passed by, and left in the gall of bitterness. This is that division, that separating fire, which Christ <hi type="italic">came to send,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.49">Luke xii. 49</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.51">51</reference>. <hi type="italic">This</hi> renders free grace the more obliging, that it is distinguishing; <hi type="italic">to us, and not to the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.14.22">John xiv. 22</reference>), nay to us, and not to those in the same field, the same mill, the same house. <div eID="gen23645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23646" type="x-p"/> When ruin came upon Jerusalem, a distinction was made by Divine Providence, according to that which had been before made by divine grace; for all the Christians among them were saved from perishing in that calamity, by the special care of Heaven. If two were at work in the field together, and one of them was a Christian, he was taken into a place of shelter, and had his life given him for a prey, while the other was left to the sword of the enemy. Nay, if but two women were grinding at the mill, if one of them belonged to Christ, though but a woman, a poor woman, a servant, she was taken to a place of safety, and the other abandoned. Thus <hi type="italic">the meek of the earth are hid in the day of the Lord's anger</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.3">Zeph. ii. 3</reference>), either in heaven, or <hi type="italic">under</hi> heaven. Note, Distinguishing preservations, in times of general destruction, are special tokens of God's favour, and ought so to be acknowledged. If we are safe when thousands fall on our right hand and our left, are not consumed when others are consumed round about us, so that we are as brands plucked out of the fire, we have reason to say, <hi type="italic">It is of the Lord's mercies,</hi> and it is a great mercy. <div eID="gen23646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23647" type="x-p"/> (2.) We may apply it to the second coming of Jesus Christ, and the separation which will be made in that day. He had said before (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.31">v. 31</reference>), that the elect will be <hi type="italic">gathered together.</hi> Here he tells us, that, in order to that, they will be distinguished from those who were nearest to them in this world; the choice and chosen ones taken to glory, the other left to perish eternally. Those who sleep in the dust of the earth, two in the same grave, their ashed mixed, shall yet arise, one to be taken to everlasting life, the other left <hi type="italic">to shame and everlasting contempt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.12.2">Dan. xii. 2</reference>. Here it is applied to them who shall be found alive. Christ will come unlooked for, will find people busy at their usual occupations, <hi type="italic">in the field, at the mill;</hi> and then, according as they are vessels of mercy prepared for glory, or vessels of wrath prepared for ruin, accordingly it will be with them; the one taken <hi type="italic">to meet the Lord and his angels in the air, to be for ever with him and them;</hi> the other left to the devil and his angels, who, when Christ has gathered out his own, will sweep up the residue. This will aggravate the condemnation of sinners that others shall be taken from the midst of them to glory, and they left behind. And it speaks abundance of comfort to the Lord's people. [1.] Are they mean and despised in the world, as the man-servant in the field, or the maid at the mill (<reference osisRef="Exod.11.5">Exod. xi. 5</reference>)? Yet they shall not be forgotten or overlooked in that day. The poor in the world, if rich in faith, are <hi type="italic">heirs of the kingdom.</hi> [2.] Are they dispersed in distant and unlikely places, where one would not expect to find the heirs of glory, <hi type="italic">in the field, at the mill?</hi> Yet the angels will find them there (hidden as Saul among the stuff, when they are to be enthroned), and fetch them thence; and well may they be said to be <hi type="italic">changed,</hi> for a very great change it will be to go to heaven from ploughing and grinding. [3.] Are they weak, and unable of themselves to move heavenward? They shall be taken, or <hi type="italic">laid hold of,</hi> as Lot was taken out of Sodom by a gracious violence, <reference osisRef="Gen.19.16">Gen. xix. 16</reference>. Those whom Christ has once apprehended and laid hold on, he will never lose his hold of. [4.] Are they intermixed with others, linked with them in the same habitations, societies, employments? Let not that discourage any true Christian; God knows how to separate between the precious and the vile, the gold and dross in the same lump, the wheat and chaff in the same floor. <div eID="gen23647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23648" type="x-p"/> III. Here is a general exhortation to us, <hi type="italic">to watch, and be ready</hi> against that day comes, enforced by divers weighty considerations, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.42">v. 42</reference>, &c. Observe, <div eID="gen23648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23649" type="x-p"/> 1. The duty required; <hi type="italic">Watch, and be ready,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.42">v. 42</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.44">44</reference>. <div eID="gen23649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23650" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">Watch therefore,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.42">v. 42</reference>. Note, It is the great duty and interest of all the disciples of Christ to watch, to be awake and keep awake, that they may mind their business. As a sinful state or way is compared to <hi type="italic">sleep,</hi> senseless and inactive (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.6">1 Thess. v. 6</reference>), so a gracious state or way is compared to <hi type="italic">watching</hi> and <hi type="italic">waking.</hi> We must watch for our Lord's coming, to us in particular at our death, <hi type="italic">after which is the judgment,</hi> that is <hi type="italic">the great day</hi> with us, the end of our time; and his coming at the end of all time to judge the world, the <hi type="italic">great day</hi> with all mankind. To watch implies not only to believe that our Lord will come, but to desire that he would come, to be often thinking of his coming, and always looking for it as sure and near, and the time of it uncertain. To watch for Christ's coming, is to maintain that gracious temper and disposition of mind which we should be willing that our Lord, when he comes, should find us in. To watch is to be aware of the first notices of his approach, that we may immediately attend his motions, and address ourselves to the duty of meeting him. Watching is supposed to be in the night, which is sleeping time; while we are in this world, it is <hi type="italic">night</hi> with us, and we must take pains to keep ourselves awake. <div eID="gen23650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23651" type="x-p"/> (2.) <hi type="italic">Be ye also ready.</hi> We wake in vain, if we do not get ready. It is not enough to <hi type="italic">look</hi> for such things; but we must therefore <hi type="italic">give diligence,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.11">2 Pet. iii. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.14">14</reference>. We have then our Lord to attend upon, and we must have our lamps ready trimmed; a cause to be tried, and we must have our plea ready drawn and signed by our Advocate; a reckoning to make up, and we must have our accounts ready stated and balanced; there is an inheritance which we then hope to enter upon, and we must have ourselves ready, made meet to partake of it, <reference osisRef="Col.1.12">Col. i. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen23651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23652" type="x-p"/> 2. The reasons to induce us to this watchfulness and diligent preparation for that day; which are two. <div eID="gen23652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23653" type="x-p"/> (1.) Because the time of our Lord's coming is very uncertain. This is the reason immediately annexed to the double exhortation (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.42">v. 42</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.44">44</reference>); and it is illustrated by a comparison, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.43">v. 43</reference>. Let us consider then, <div eID="gen23653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23654" type="x-p"/> [1.] That <hi type="italic">we know not what hour he will come,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.42">v. 42</reference>. We know not <hi type="italic">the day of our death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.27.2">Gen. xxvii. 2</reference>. We may know that we have but <hi type="italic">a little time to live (The time of my departure is at hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.6">2 Tim. iv. 6</reference>); but we cannot know that we have a long time to live, for our souls are continually in our hands; nor can we know how little a time we have to live, for it may prove less than we expect; much less do we know the time fixed for the general judgment. Concerning both we are kept at uncertainty, that we may, every day, expect that which may come any day; may never boast of a year's continuance (<reference osisRef="Jas.4.13">James iv. 13</reference>), no, nor of tomorrow's return, as if it were ours, <reference osisRef="Prov.27.1">Prov. xxvii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.12.20">Luke xii. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen23654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23655" type="x-p"/> [2.] That he may <hi type="italic">come at such an hour as we think not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.44">v. 44</reference>. Though there be such uncertainty in the time, there is none in the thing itself: though we know not <hi type="italic">when</hi> he will come, we are sure he <hi type="italic">will</hi> come. His parting word was, <hi type="italic">Surely I come quickly;</hi> his saying, "I come <hi type="italic">surely,</hi>" obliges us to expect him: his saying "I come <hi type="italic">quickly.</hi>" obliges us to be always expecting him; for it keeps us in a state of expectancy. <hi type="italic">In such an hour as you think not,</hi> that is, such an hour as they who are unready and unprepared, think not (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.50">v. 50</reference>); nay, such an hour as the most lively expectants perhaps thought least likely. The bridegroom came when the wise were slumbering. It is agreeable to our present state, that we should be under the influence of a constant and general expectation, rather than that of particular presages and prognostications, which we are sometimes tempted vainly to desire and wish for. <div eID="gen23655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23656" type="x-p"/> [3.] That the children of this world are thus wise in their generation, that, when they know of a danger approaching, they will keep awake, and stand on their guard against it. This he shows in a particular instance, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.43">v. 43</reference>. If the master of a house had notice that a thief would come such a night, and such a watch of the night (for they divided the night into four watches, allowing three hours to each), and would make an attempt upon his house, though it were the midnight-watch, when he was most sleepy, yet he would be up, and listen to every noise in every corner, and be ready to give him a warm reception. Now, though we know not <hi type="italic">just when</hi> our Lord will come, yet, knowing that he <hi type="italic">will</hi> come, and come quickly, and without any other warning than what he hath given in his word, it concerns us to watch always. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> We have every one of us a house to keep, which lies exposed, in which all we are worth is laid up: that house is our own souls, which we must <hi type="italic">keep with all diligence. Secondly,</hi> The day of the Lord comes <hi type="italic">by surprise, as a thief in the night.</hi> Christ chooses to come when he is least expected, that the triumphs of his enemies may be turned into the greater shame, and the fears of his friends into the greater joy. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> If Christ, when he comes, finds us asleep and unready, our house will be broken up, and we shall lose all we are worth, not as by a thief unjustly, but as by a just and legal process; death and judgment will seize upon all we have, to our irreparable damage and utter undoing. Therefore be ready, <hi type="italic">be ye also ready;</hi> as ready at all times as the good man of the house would be at the hour when he expected the thief: we must put on the armour of God, that we may not only stand in that evil day, but, as more than conquerors, may divide the spoil. <div eID="gen23656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23657" type="x-p"/> (2.) Because the issue of our Lord's coming will be very happy and comfortable to those that shall be found ready, but very dismal and dreadful to those that shall not, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.45">v. 45</reference>, &c. This is represented by the different state of good and bad servants, when their lord comes to reckon with them. It is likely to be well or ill with us to eternity, according as we are found ready or unready at that day; for Christ comes <hi type="italic">to render to every man according to his works.</hi> Now this parable, with which the chapter closes, is applicable to all Christians, who are in profession and obligation God's servants; but it seems especially intended as a warning to ministers; for the servant spoken of is a <hi type="italic">steward.</hi> Now observe what Christ here saith, <div eID="gen23657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23658" type="x-p"/> [1.] Concerning the <hi type="italic">good servant;</hi> he shows here what he is—<hi type="italic">a ruler of the household;</hi> what, being so, he should be—<hi type="italic">faithful</hi> and <hi type="italic">wise;</hi> and what, if he be so, he shall be eternally-<hi type="italic">blessed.</hi> Here are good instructions and encouragements to the ministers of Christ. <div eID="gen23658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23659" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> We have here his place and office. He is one <hi type="italic">whom the Lord has made ruler over his household, to give them meat in due season.</hi> Note, 1. The church of Christ is his household, or family, standing in relation to him as the Father and Master of it. It is <hi type="italic">the household of God,</hi> a family named from Christ, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.15">Eph. iii. 15</reference>. 2. Gospel ministers are appointed <hi type="italic">rulers</hi> in this household; not at princes (Christ has entered a caveat against that), but as stewards, or other subordinate officers; not as lords, but as guides; not to prescribe new ways, but to show and lead in the ways that Christ has appointed: that is the signification of the <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hegoumenoi</hi></hi>, which we translate, <hi type="italic">having rule over you</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.17">Heb. xiii. 17</reference>); as <hi type="italic">overseers,</hi> not to cut out new work, but to direct in, and quicken to, the work which Christ has ordered; that is the signification of <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">episkopoi</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">bishops.</hi> They are rulers by Christ; what power they have is derived from him, and none may take it from them, or abridge it to them; he is one whom <hi type="italic">the Lord has made ruler;</hi> Christ has the <hi type="italic">making</hi> of ministers. They are rulers <hi type="italic">under</hi> Christ, and act in subordination to him; and rulers <hi type="italic">for</hi> Christ, for the advancement of his kingdom. 3. The work of gospel ministers is to give to Christ's household their meat in due season, as stewards, and therefore they have the keys delivered to them. (1.) Their work is <hi type="italic">to give,</hi> not take to themselves (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.8">Ezek. xxxiv. 8</reference>), but give to the family what the Master has bought, to <hi type="italic">dispense</hi> what Christ has <hi type="italic">purchased.</hi> And to ministers it is said, that <hi type="italic">it is more blessed to give than to receive,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.20.35">Acts xx. 35</reference>. (2.) It is to give <hi type="italic">meat;</hi> not to give <hi type="italic">law</hi> (that is Christ's work), but to deliver those doctrines to the church which, if duly digested, will be nourishment to souls. They must give, not the poison of false doctrines, not the stones of hard and unprofitable doctrines, but the meat that is <hi type="italic">sound</hi> and <hi type="italic">wholesome.</hi> (3.) It must be given <hi type="italic">in due season,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">en kairo</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">while there is time for it;</hi> when eternity comes, it will be too late; we must <hi type="italic">work while it is day:</hi> or <hi type="italic">in time,</hi> that is, whenever any opportunity offers itself; or in the stated time, time after time, according as the duty of every day requires. <div eID="gen23659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23660" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> His right discharge of this office. The good servant, if thus preferred, will be a good <hi type="italic">steward;</hi> for, <div eID="gen23660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23661" type="x-p"/> 1. He is <hi type="italic">faithful;</hi> stewards must be so, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.2">1 Cor. iv. 2</reference>. He that is <hi type="italic">trusted,</hi> must be trusty; and the greater the trust is, the more is expected from them. It is a great good thing that is committed to <hi type="italic">ministers</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.14">2 Tim. i. 14</reference>); and they must be faithful, as Moses was, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.2">Heb. iii. 2</reference>. Christ counts those ministers, and those only, that are <hi type="italic">faithful,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.12">1 Tim. i. 12</reference>. A faithful minister of Jesus Christ is one that sincerely designs his master's honour, not his own; delivers <hi type="italic">the whole counsel of God,</hi> not his own fancies and conceits; follows Christ's institutions and adheres to them; regards the meanest, reproves the greatest, and doth not respect persons. <div eID="gen23661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23662" type="x-p"/> 2. He is wise to understand his duty and the proper season of it; and in guiding of the flock there is need, not only of the integrity of the heart, but the skilfulness of the hands. Honesty may suffice for a good <hi type="italic">servant,</hi> but wisdom is necessary to a <hi type="italic">good steward;</hi> for it is profitable to direct. <div eID="gen23662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23663" type="x-p"/> 3. He is doing; <hi type="italic">so doing</hi> as his office requires. The ministry is a good work, and they whose office it is, have always something to do; they must not indulge themselves in ease, nor leave the work undone, or carelessly turn it off to others, but be doing, and doing to the purpose—<hi type="italic">so doing,</hi> giving meat to the household, minding their own business, and not meddling with that which is foreign; <hi type="italic">so doing</hi> as the Master has appointed, as the office imports, and as the case of the family requires; not <hi type="italic">talking,</hi> but <hi type="italic">doing.</hi> It was the motto Mr. Perkins used, <hi type="italic">Minister verbi es—You are a minister of the word.</hi> Not only <hi type="italic">Age—Be doing;</hi> but <hi type="italic">Hoc age—Be so doing.</hi> <div eID="gen23663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23664" type="x-p"/> 4. He is <hi type="italic">found doing</hi> when his Master comes; which intimates, (1.) Constancy at his work. At what hour soever his Master comes, he is found busy at the work of the day. Ministers should not leave empty spaces in their time, lest their Lord should come in one of those empty spaces. As with a good God the end of one mercy is the beginning of another, so with a good man, a good minister, the end of one duty is the beginning of another. When Calvin was persuaded to remit his ministerial labours, he answered, with some resentment, "What, would you have my Master find me idle?" (2.) Perseverance in his work till the Lord come. <hi type="italic">Hold fast till then,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.2.25">Rev. ii. 25</reference>. <hi type="italic">Continue in these things,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.16">1 Tim. iv. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.14">vi. 14</reference>. Endure to the end. <div eID="gen23664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23665" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The recompence of reward intended him for this, in three things. <div eID="gen23665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23666" type="x-p"/> 1. He shall be taken notice of. This is intimated in these words, Who then is that <hi type="italic">faithful and wise servant?</hi> Which supposes that there are but few who answer this character; such an interpreter is <hi type="italic">one of a thousand,</hi> such a faithful and wise <hi type="italic">steward.</hi> Those who thus distinguish themselves now by humility, diligence, and sincerity in their work, Christ will in the great day both dignify and distinguish by the glory conferred on them. <div eID="gen23666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23667" type="x-p"/> 2. He shall be blessed? <hi type="italic">Blessed is that servant;</hi> and Christ's pronouncing him blessed makes him so. All the dead that die in the Lord are blessed, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.13">Rev. xiv. 13</reference>. But there is a peculiar blessedness secured to them that approve themselves faithful stewards, and are found so doing. Next to the honour of those who die in the field of battle, suffering for Christ as the martyrs, is the honour of those that die in the field of service, ploughing, and sowing, and reaping, for Christ. <div eID="gen23667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23668" type="x-p"/> 3. He shall be preferred (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.47">v. 47</reference>); <hi type="italic">He shall make him ruler over all his goods.</hi> The allusion is to the way of great men, who, if the stewards of their house conduct themselves well in that place, commonly prefer them to be the managers of their estates; thus Joseph was preferred in the house of Potiphar, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.4">Gen. xxix. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.6">6</reference>. But the greatest honour which the kindest master ever did to his most tried servants in this world, is nothing to that weight of glory which the Lord Jesus will confer upon his faithful watchful servants in the world to come.
